Korea and Vietnam, 1950–1973

Eleven battles from Task Force Smith at Osan in 1950 to Hamburger Hill in 1969: the first American fight in Korea, the Marines at Fox Hill, the perimeter at Chipyong-ni, the Commonwealth brigade at Kapyong, the hills of Heartbreak Ridge and Pork Chop, the landing zone at X-Ray, Hill 875 at Dak To, Hill 861A at Khe Sanh, the street fighting in Hue and the A Shau valley. Every rule is in the Rules; this book holds the armies' figures for both wars, the wound tables their battles roll on, the battlefields, and a rifle squad in Vietnam followed through one night.

The battlefields: Task Force Smith at Osan 1950, Fox Hill at Toktong Pass 1950, The perimeter at Chipyong-ni 1951, Hill 504 and the valley at Kapyong 1951, Hill 931 on Heartbreak Ridge 1951, Pork Chop Hill 1953, Landing zone X-Ray 1965, Hill 875 1967, Hill 861A 1968, Hue: the new city 1968, Hamburger Hill 1969.

The period's fighting

This book covers two wars in Asia: Korea, from 1950 to 1953, and Vietnam, from 1965 to 1973, the years when American and Australian armies fought there. Its battles run from Task Force Smith at Osan in July 1950 to Hamburger Hill in May 1969. Both wars were fought for hills and ridges by infantry with the full weight of guns and aircraft behind them, and in both the helicopter carried the wounded to the surgeon.

Armies

The United States fought both wars with the draft. Between June 1950 and the armistice of 1953 Selective Service inducted over 1.5 million men; about 1.3 million more volunteered, most of them for the Navy or the Air Force. The act of 1951 lowered the age of induction to 18 and a half and made service 24 months. For Vietnam, from August 1964 to February 1973, the tables count 1,857,304 men inducted. College students could be deferred. On 1 December 1969 a lottery by birthday set the order of call for men born from 1944 to 1950. The last draft call went out on 7 December 1972, and in January 1973 the draft ended.

Australia also sent conscripts. Its national servicemen were chosen by a birthday ballot of twenty-year-olds: marbles, each standing for two birthdays, were drawn from a barrel. The scheme ran from November 1964 to December 1972. Of 804,286 young men registered, the Australian War Memorial counts 63,735 who served in the Army. The Department of Veterans' Affairs says more than 15,300 of them served in Vietnam, and more than 200 national servicemen died overseas.

In Korea the American divisions of 1950 were short of men. In August 1950 President Syngman Rhee and General Douglas MacArthur agreed, by word of mouth only, to put Korean soldiers into American units. These were the KATUSA, the Korean Augmentation to the United States Army. Some volunteered and some were taken by force; before the Inchon landing the 7th Infantry Division took 313 men from Busan. In all 43,660 served with the Americans, and 11,365 were killed or missing.

In October 1950 the Chinese came into the war as the People's Volunteer Army (PVA). The Center of Military History's account says over 300,000 men in 30 divisions were in Korea by 6 November, while MacArthur's intelligence staff counted 34,500. Experts had expected them to be poorly armed, poorly led and badly supplied. They were short of supplies but well motivated and hardened by years of war. They attacked at night, often to bugles, and set roadblocks behind the Americans.

In Vietnam the enemy came in two forms. The National Liberation Front (NLF), founded in the South on 20 December 1960, was the Viet Cong of the Americans; its army was the Liberation Army of South Vietnam. It fought under Hanoi's direction, and Vietnam's official history calls it a part of the North's army. The People's Army of Vietnam (PAVN) sent its regulars south down the Ho Chi Minh Trail, run from 1959 by Group 559; about 200,000 went south before the Tet offensive of 1968. Tet cost the Front dearly. "Tet cost us half our forces," one of its leaders, Trương Như Tảng, later wrote.

Arms

The American in Korea carried the M1 Garand, the self-loading rifle of 1939-45; a "winter trigger" let him fire it in gloves. By Vietnam it had given way to the M14, and from March 1965 the Army began to issue the M16. It was light, fired a small 5.56 mm round from a 20-round magazine, and in its first years jammed. The powder fouled it, it came without cleaning kits, and its chamber was not chromed, so spent cases stuck. A newspaper story of 26 March 1967 led to a Congressional inquiry. The M16A1, standardised in February 1967, had a chromed chamber and came with cleaning kits. Against it the Viet Cong and the PAVN carried the Kalashnikov, most often the Chinese copy, the Type 56. American reports had said early on that men with the heavier M14 could not carry enough rounds to match its fire.

In Korea the Americans had the Browning Automatic Rifle and the belt-fed Browning machine guns of the last war. In Vietnam the M60 machine gun, the "Pig", was meant to replace both. It fired 550 to 650 rounds a minute and weighed over 10 kg, and riflemen carried belts and spare barrels for it.

Fragments of mortar bombs, artillery shells, grenades and mines did much of the wounding; on Hamburger Hill, Galloway says, about half the American losses. "We must expend steel and fire, not men," said General James Van Fleet in May 1951. On Hamburger Hill in 1969 the guns fired some 20,000 rounds at one mountain. Napalm, a jellied petrol, came from the air. The US Air Force dropped more than 30,000 tons of it on Korea, and some 388,000 short tons of American napalm bombs fell in South-East Asia from 1963 to 1973.

The helicopter changed both wars. In Korea small Bell H-13s carried two patients in litters outside the cabin. By Vietnam the United States had some 4,000 helicopters in the theatre, and the Bell UH-1, the Huey, carried the infantry into battle and the wounded out.

Battles

The first year in Korea was a war of movement, south to Pusan, north to the Yalu and back. Talks for a cease-fire opened at Kaesong on 10 July 1951, and while they went on, the line settled across the peninsula. Both sides dug in along the ridges: trenches, bunkers and caves on the Main Line of Resistance, with outposts on the hills in front. Each outpost of the Nevada Cities in March 1953 was held by a platoon of about 40 Marines and two Navy corpsmen. Vegas, the tallest, stood about 1,200 m beyond the line. Patrols and raids went out by night; the big fights were for single hills, held for the view they gave. The armistice was signed on 27 July 1953 and set a demilitarised zone 4 km wide along the front.

Reckless

In October 1952 Lieutenant Eric Pedersen of the 5th Marines' recoilless rifle platoon paid $250 of his own money for a chestnut mare at the Seoul racecourse. The Marines named her Reckless, after the rifle, and trained her to carry its 24-pound shells up to the guns and the wounded down. The figures usually given for Outpost Vegas in March 1953, and repeated by the National Museum of the Marine Corps, are 51 trips alone in one day, 386 rounds and more than 35 miles; the museum ties them to no source, and much else told of her is unit legend. What is sure is that she was wounded twice, was made a sergeant in 1954 and a staff sergeant by General Randolph Pate in 1959, and died in May 1968.

In Vietnam there was no front. Under General William Westmoreland, in 1966 and 1967, American units went out on search and destroy: companies and battalions moved out from their bases to find the enemy, fight him and count his dead. The body count became the measure of success. Units went in by helicopter to a landing zone, often a clearing just big enough for a few Hueys, and sometimes came under fire as they landed. The guns that supported them sat on a fire support base: a battery of six howitzers, two helicopter pads, an aid station and an infantry company to guard them, out in the country. At first they moved every two days or so; later many became small forts. After Hamburger Hill the Americans were told to spare their own men, and the war passed slowly to the South Vietnamese.

Wounds and medicine

The Mobile Army Surgical Hospital (MASH) was the new hospital of Korea: 60 beds under canvas, 5 to 40 km behind the front. The 8076th had 10 doctors, 12 nurses and 89 enlisted men, and once took in over 600 casualties in a day. Most wounded still came by jeep and truck ambulance. A seriously wounded man who reached a MASH alive, King and Jatoi write, had a better than 97% chance of living.

The Air Force flew the first helicopter ambulances in July 1950. The Army's 2nd Helicopter Detachment began work on 1 January 1951. By the armistice, Dorland and Nanney count, Army helicopters had flown about 17,700 casualties, with only eleven aircraft at the peak. They brought 10 to 20% of those who reached the MASHs.

In Vietnam the helicopter ambulance became the Dustoff, from the call sign the 57th Medical Detachment chose in 1963. Unarmed Hueys marked with red crosses flew in to the fighting, and where they could not land they lowered a hoist through the trees. Dorland and Nanney say they carried almost 900,000 American and allied sick and wounded. The Vietnam Archive at Texas Tech says most wounded men were in a hospital within 35 minutes; another account gives an average of 2.8 hours. Either way the time from wound to surgeon was shorter than in any war before. Of the wounded who reached treatment, 2.6% died, against 4.5% in 1939-45; the figure for Korea is given as 2.5%.

When I have your wounded

Major Charles Kelly took command of the 57th Medical Detachment in January 1964 and moved south to Soc Trang, in the Mekong Delta. He held that ambulance helicopters should fly unarmed and go in under fire. On 1 July 1964 he flew to a field south of Vinh Long to pick up a wounded American adviser. The men on the ground told him to leave: the landing zone was under fire. Most accounts give his answer as "When I have your wounded"; Peter Arnett had it as "I'll move when I have your wounded with me." A single bullet came through the open cargo door and struck him in the heart. He was the 149th American to die in Vietnam. His unit flew on as he had taught it, and it became the Dustoff way.

Surgeons learned to save legs. In 1939-45 a torn main artery was tied off, and about half of those limbs were lost. In Korea, from December 1951, John Howard's surgical research team at the 46th MASH and the young surgeon Edward Jahnke began to repair arteries instead. They got six Potts clamps, one for each MASH, and taught a pair of surgeons from each how to use them in a day. Carl Hughes reported an amputation rate of 13% over 304 repairs. In Vietnam limbs were saved in 87% of cases, Rich found.

Men began to wear body armour again. In Korea the M1951 vest, nylon with plates of a fibreglass called Doron, weighed just under 8 pounds. The Army's nylon M1952A reached the front only late in 1952, about 26,161 of them by July 1953. In a field test in Korea in 1952 a trial vest stopped 75.7% of fragments but only 24.4% of bullets. The Vietnam vests could not stop a Kalashnikov round either, and in the heat men mostly wore them in fixed positions and convoys.

Disease came with the country. In Vietnam malaria put an average of 26.7 men in every 1,000 into hospital each year, against 11.2 in Korea; in December 1965 the Army's rate reached 98.4, and in some units in the Ia Drang valley 600. In Korea the enemy was the cold. At the Chosin Reservoir in November and December 1950 the temperature fell to minus 30 °F (about minus 34 °C) and below. About 8,000 men there were frostbitten. Canteens and rations froze, and fires were forbidden. Of the frostbite cases at Percy Jones hospital in Michigan, about 90% were of the feet. Surgeons tried to save what they could, often taking only fingertips rather than whole hands.

Women

In both wars American women served as nurses. Some 540 nurses of the Army Nurse Corps served in Korea, in the MASHs and the hospitals of Korea and Japan. They triaged, started transfusions and penicillin, and sutured wounds. The Navy had 3,081 active and 1,702 reserve nurses in the war, on hospital ships and evacuation aircraft. One Army nurse, Genevieve Smith, died on her way to her post; the National Archives finds no woman nurse killed by the enemy.

Over 11,000 American servicewomen served in the Vietnam war, most of them nurses. Eight died: seven Army nurses and one of the Air Force. Over 340 Australian nurses, military and civilian, served with their forces, 43 of them from the Royal Australian Army Nursing Corps.

Ward 4

Sharon Lane trained as a nurse at Aultman Hospital in Canton, Ohio, and joined the Army Nurse Corps Reserve in April 1968. After a year on the tuberculosis and cardiac wards at Fitzsimons General Hospital in Denver, she reached the 312th Evacuation Hospital at Chu Lai on 29 April 1969. She worked on the Vietnamese ward, which took civilians, soldiers and prisoners, and in her off-duty hours in the surgical intensive care unit. On 8 June 1969 a 122 mm rocket struck between the huts of Ward 4. The fragments killed her and a Vietnamese child. She was 25, and had been in Vietnam 41 days. She was the only American servicewoman killed by enemy fire in the war.

On the other side women also fought. At least 1.5 million women served in the North's forces. Women made up as much as 70% of the Youth Shock Brigades on the Ho Chi Minh Trail, who built and mended the roads, worked as guides, defused bombs and nursed the wounded. In the South, Nguyễn Thị Định, a co-founder of the NLF, became its deputy commander. Bến Tre province alone counted over 3,000 women guerrillas in 1961, the "long-haired army". Võ Thị Mô was second in command of a battalion near Cu Chi. Đặng Thùy Trâm, a surgeon, treated the wounded of the Front and the PAVN from 1966 until she was killed in 1970; her diaries, published in 2005, sold over 300,000 copies in a year.

For the GM

Expect a fight in Korea or Vietnam to be for a hill, and to be decided by fire. Fragments from mortars, shells and grenades do most of the wounding, and a man in a bunker or a deep hole is far safer than one in the open. The enemy fights at night and close, where the guns cannot help the Americans. A wounded American's chances are better than in any earlier war: the aidman, then a helicopter, then a surgeon within an hour or two, with whole blood, antibiotics and, from 1952, a repaired artery. A wounded Chinese, North Korean or North Vietnamese soldier has no helicopter, and must be carried. In Korea cold will take as many men as the enemy; in Vietnam, mosquitoes and the heat.

What is switched on

All four modules but the first: Modern fire, Armour and mines, and Air and night devices, with helicopters and landing by air from Vietnam on, and night vision (infrared searchlights) in Vietnam. The wounded go out by helicopter where a landing zone and a helicopter are left, as the Rules' After the battle says; else by motor ambulance. Wounds heal and fester as the Rules' Recovery says: it does not yet count the antibiotics of these wars.

Trouble at work

Korean War (1950-1953)

d10 Trouble
1 MPs search his kit and find goods or money he can't explain.
2 A surprise MPC conversion day: whatever old MPC he holds is worthless.
3 Shelling or a night raid hits the work site.
4 He walks into an unmarked friendly minefield.
5 The pay never comes: the boss pocketed the payroll.
6 A refugee family begs him to get them south.
7 Accused of working for the North: counter-intelligence asks questions.
8 Typhus or frostbite: a week lost.
9 R&R goes bad: robbed, or brawling with the shore patrol.
10 A Korean co-worker vanishes, and his family thinks he knows where.

Vietnam War (1965-1973)

d10 Trouble
1 A CID inquiry into currency or PX goods.
2 A surprise MPC conversion day: locals holding old MPC beg him to swap it.
3 A rocket or sapper attack on the site.
4 The VC tax collector demands a share, or else.
5 A road mine or booby trap on the way to work.
6 His pay is skimmed by a camp commander or a boss.
7 Heroin or a bad bar fight costs a week and his name.
8 Inflation: wages buy a fifth less this month.
9 The aircraft is shot up: walk out through hostile ground.
10 A co-worker is VC, and he knows that he knows.

What each skill is for

Korean War (1950-1953)

Skill Use Usually Against Success Failure Fumble
Persuade Haggle: Beat down a price. Ordinary the seller (Persuade) A tenth off (a quarter on a critical). The list price. No sale today.
Persuade Find a billet: Talk a village or a householder into a bed and a meal. Ordinary the householder or headman (Presence) Fed and bedded tonight: no keep to pay. He pays his keep, or sleeps rough. The village turns against the party: trouble.
Persuade Talk past a guard: Get by a sentry, a gate or the provost without the right papers. Hard the sentry or provost (Wits) Through. Turned back. Held as a deserter or a spy.
Persuade Question a prisoner: Get a prisoner or a local to talk. Ordinary the prisoner (Nerve) He tells what he knows (the GM decides how much is true). Nothing. He lies, and is believed.
Command Drive a hard task: Get men to do something hard and tiring: dig all night, march on after dark, cross a river. Ordinary — Done. Done slowly, or only half. They refuse.
Command Keep order: Stop plunder, drinking or a mutinous mood. Hard — They obey. Some slip away to it. They turn on him.
Letters Read or write: Read an order, a letter or a map's names; write a report. Easy — Read or written. Slowly, or with mistakes. He gets it wrong and does not know it.
Letters Forge a pass: Make a pass, an order or a billeting ticket that will be believed. Hard whoever checks it (Watch) It passes. Doubted: Talk past a guard instead. Seen through: held as a deserter or a spy.
Craft Mend kit: Mend a weapon, harness, boots, a cart or a radio set; a day's work. Ordinary — Mended. Not yet: another day. Ruined.
Craft Make something: Make ladders, a raft, a shelter, snowshoes or a litter from what is to hand. Ordinary — Made. Takes twice as long. It fails when it is used.
Drive Drive under pressure: Drive off the road, at night without lights, or under fire. Ordinary — Through. Slowed or lost. Ditched or overturned.
Fieldcraft Track: Follow men or animals. Ordinary the men being followed (Stealth) On their trail. Lost it. On the wrong trail.
Fieldcraft Find the way: Cross country without roads or a guide; at night, hard. Ordinary — On the way. Half a day lost. Lost: a day, or into the enemy.
Fieldcraft Hunt or gather: Find food or water for himself in the country. Ordinary — Fed today: no keep to pay. Nothing found. Something that makes him ill.
Watch Spot: See an ambush, a man hiding, a trap or a thing out of place. Ordinary whoever is hiding (Stealth) Seen. Missed. Sure there is nothing there.
Watch Search: Search a house, a body or a baggage wagon. Easy — Found what there is. Missed it. Missed it and left traces.
Stealth Sneak: Get past sentries, into a camp or away from one. Ordinary the sentries (Watch) Unseen. Seen, but not yet caught. Walks into them.
Stealth Steal: Lift a purse, a horse or rations unseen. Hard the owner or the guard (Watch) Taken. Not taken. Caught in the act: the provost.
Leechcraft Diagnose: Tell what a sick man has, and whether it will spread. Ordinary — Named: the GM tells which sickness. Unsure. Wrong.
Signals Get through: Raise another station, mend a line or a set, or send a message in code. Ordinary — Through. Not yet: try again next hour. The set or line is out until mended.
Strength Force or carry: Force a door, lift a beam, carry a wounded man. Ordinary — Done. Not alone. Strained: a step of fatigue.
Agility Climb or jump: Climb a wall, jump a ditch, keep his feet on ice. Ordinary — Over. Not this way. Falls: roll a fall as a wound.
Endurance Endure: Keep going: swim, go without sleep, hold out in the cold. Ordinary — Holds out. A step of fatigue. Collapses, or goes under.
Wits Notice or remember: Recall a face, a road or a password; work something out. Ordinary — Yes. No. Remembers it wrong.
Nerve Keep his head: Stay calm out of a fight: under shelling in a dugout, at a hanging, before an officer. Ordinary — Steady. Shaken: −10 to his next check. Breaks: runs, freezes or lashes out.
Presence Impress: Stare a man down, make a first impression, be remembered. Ordinary the other man (Presence) He gives way. No effect. Made an enemy.

Stealth Steal: Lift a purse, a horse or rations unseen. Hard the owner or the guard (Watch) Taken. Not taken. Caught in the act: the provost.
Leechcraft Diagnose: Tell what a sick man has, and whether it will spread. Ordinary — Named: the GM tells which sickness. Unsure. Wrong.
Signals Get through: Raise another station, mend a line or a set, or send a message in code. Ordinary — Through. Not yet: try again next hour. The set or line is out until mended.
Strength Force or carry: Force a door, lift a beam, carry a wounded man. Ordinary — Done. Not alone. Strained: a step of fatigue.
Agility Climb or jump: Climb a wall, jump a ditch, keep his feet on ice. Ordinary — Over. Not this way. Falls: roll a fall as a wound.
Endurance Endure: Keep going: swim, go without sleep, hold out in the cold. Ordinary — Holds out. A step of fatigue. Collapses, or goes under.
Wits Notice or remember: Recall a face, a road or a password; work something out. Ordinary — Yes. No. Remembers it wrong.
Nerve Keep his head: Stay calm out of a fight: under shelling in a dugout, at a hanging, before an officer. Ordinary — Steady. Shaken: −10 to his next check. Breaks: runs, freezes or lashes out.
Presence Impress: Stare a man down, make a first impression, be remembered. Ordinary the other man (Presence) He gives way. No effect. Made an enemy.

Each battle rolls its wounds on a table built from the record of that war, and these are the notes on where each one comes from. The tables themselves are in the printed tables and the wound roller. A gameplay-adjusted table is re-weighted from bone evidence to stand for every blow that landed, not only the ones that marked bone; an evidence table is the record itself.

Battlefields

Each battlefield lays out on the field map under Battlefield. What follows is what the field and its phases hold, and, briefly, what happened there.

Task Force Smith at Osan, 5 July 1950

  • The armies: United Nations and North Koreans.
  • Fought for: the saddle where the road crosses the ridge, attacked by the North Koreans.
  • The field: 220 by 110 hexes of 10 m, about 2,200 by 950 m, north at the top.
  • The weather: Overcast, calm or light air from the south.
  • Wounds: Korea 1950-53 - hospitalized wounded.
  • On the travel map: Osan, 1950 (Suwon to P'yongt'aek), at the saddle north of Osan (Jukmiryeong).

The campaign

Korea had been divided at the 38th parallel since 1945. At 04:00 on 25 June 1950 the North Korean People's Army attacked across it from coast to coast. Half the force went down the Uijongbu corridor towards Seoul. The Center of Military History puts the assault force at about 90,000 men: seven infantry divisions, an armoured brigade and smaller units, with about 150 Soviet T-34 tanks. The South Korean army had 95,000 men and no tanks. By the end of June it could account for only 22,000.

Seoul fell on 28 June to the North Korean 3rd and 4th Divisions; the Han River bridges were blown early, cutting off much of the South Korean army. The UN Security Council called for a cease-fire on 25 June and on 27 June asked its members to help. On 29 June President Truman let the Army secure a port and airfield at Pusan and agreed to send two divisions from Japan.

On 30 June MacArthur ordered the 24th Infantry Division to Korea. At 20:00 on 1 July Lieutenant Colonel Charles B. Smith, commanding the 1st Battalion, 21st Infantry, was alerted at Camp Wood, near Kumamoto. He took two understrength rifle companies, B and C, with recoilless rifles and mortars. 406 of his men flew from Itazuke to Pusan that day. Appleman says about one man in six had been in combat. They went by train to Taejon, arriving at 08:00 on 2 July, and then north to P'yongt'aek and Ansong.

On 4 July A Battery, 52nd Field Artillery Battalion, under Lieutenant Colonel Miller O. Perry, joined Smith at P'yongt'aek. Brigadier General George B. Barth told Smith to take up the positions he had chosen near Osan. The force left a little after midnight in commandeered trucks; the 12 miles took two and a half hours in blackout. At about 03:00 on 5 July the men began to dig in. It was raining.

The places

  • Suwon: the town to the north, down whose road the North Koreans came.
  • The ridge north of Osan: about three miles north of the town, across the road at right angles; its highest point about 300 feet above the paddies.
  • The saddle: the low point where the highway crossed the ridge. The memorial there takes its name, Jukmiryeong, from the pass.
  • The knob west of the highway: held by one platoon of B Company, and taken by the North Koreans at 12:30.
  • The railroad: on the right, bending away to the east almost a mile from the road. C Company's right was bent back along a finger ridge west of it.
  • The battery position: about 2,000 yards behind the infantry, four howitzers 150 yards west of the highway, with a fifth halfway forward to fire on the saddle.
  • Osan: the town behind the line, where the vehicles waited and where three tanks blocked the road south in the afternoon.
  • P'yongt'aek and Ansong: 15 and 20 miles to the south and south-east, where the force came from and its survivors went.
  • The UN Forces First Battle Memorial: on the ridge today, with the Jukmiryeong Peace Park and museum, opened in July 2020.

The leaders

  • Charles B. Smith (American, 1st Battalion, 21st Infantry): commanded the task force. He later said he stayed in the position too long.
  • Miller O. Perry (American, 52nd Field Artillery Battalion): commanded the battery. Wounded in the right leg, he refused to be evacuated.
  • George B. Barth (American, 24th Infantry Division): sent Smith forward from P'yongt'aek and recorded the first round at 08:16.
  • William F. Dean (American, 24th Infantry Division): chose Smith's battalion to go first.
  • Ollie D. Connor (American, second lieutenant): fired 22 bazooka rockets at the tanks from about 15 yards.
  • Raymond "Bodie" Adams (American, first lieutenant): knocked out a machine gun with a grenade thrown about 40 yards during the withdrawal.
  • Lee Kwon Mu (North Korean, 4th Division): led the infantry column, by Wikipedia's account.
  • 107th Tank Regiment, 105th Armored Division (North Korean, the tanks): no source read for this page names its commander. Wikipedia lists a Ryu Kyong-su among the North Korean commanders without saying which unit he led.

The battle

Times here are local, as Appleman gives them. At the ridge were 540 Americans: 17 officers and 389 men of infantry, and 9 officers and 125 men of artillery. The battery had about 1,200 rounds but only 6 anti-tank (HEAT) rounds. A little after 07:00 Smith saw movement near Suwon. Eight tanks came first and then others in groups of about four, 33 in all. At 08:16 the howitzers opened fire at about 4,000 yards, without effect. The recoilless rifles held their fire until 700 yards and hit the leading tanks, which kept on. The forward howitzer, firing HEAT, stopped the two leading tanks, and one burned. A later tank destroyed that gun. By 09:00 the last tank had passed the infantry, and about 20 infantrymen had been killed or wounded.

The tanks cut the telephone wire to the guns. The radios were wet, and by 11:00 the battery had lost touch with the infantry. The tanks drove past the battery, the last by 10:15. One was stopped by a shell in its tracks. Sergeant Edwin A. Eversole's bazooka round bounced off another. In all four tanks were destroyed or stopped and three slightly damaged. Perry and one other man were the only wounded at the battery.

About an hour after the tanks, a column some six miles long came out of Suwon: three tanks, then trucks, then marching infantry. It was the 16th and 18th Regiments of the North Korean 4th Division. At about 11:45, when the trucks were about 1,000 yards off, the mortars and machine guns opened fire and set them burning. About 1,000 men got down and spread out to both flanks. At about 12:30 they took the knob west of the highway, and the B Company platoon there moved east of the road.

At about 14:30 Smith decided to go. The enemy was on both flanks with a large reserve on the road, small-arms ammunition was nearly gone, he had no communications and no help was coming. The companies leapfrogged off the ridge and down the finger ridge west of the railroad: C Company first, then the medics, battalion headquarters and B Company. B Company's 2nd Platoon never got the order. The men left the recoilless rifles, mortars and machine guns and carried only rifles with two or three clips. Most of the losses came now, as the groups crossed the open ground under fire.

About 25 to 30 men on litters had to be left behind. A medical sergeant volunteered to stay with them. The walking wounded went with the companies, but many fell behind when fire broke up the groups. Smith found the battery with all its guns still working. The gunners took out the sights and breech locks and drove off. At the south edge of Osan three tanks blocked the road, so the column turned back through the town and went east on a dirt road, with about 100 infantrymen on the trucks. It reached Ansong after dark. The North Koreans took the ridge and did not follow. Survivors counted at Ch'onan on 6 July came to 185, and 65 more came in with Captain Richard Dashmer.

Where the accounts disagree

  • The clock. Appleman does not say which clock. Korea kept GMT+9, but South Korea tried a summer time of GMT+10 in 1948 to 1951; no source read says whether the Army used it.
  • When the tanks were seen. Appleman notes that Smith told him about 07:00 but said 07:45 in an interview on 7 July; Eversole recalled 07:45, Barth about 08:00, and a telephone report 08:18. Wikipedia gives about 07:30.
  • How many men. Appleman gives 540; the Center of Military History's brochure, about 500; the Army's 2019 article, the 406 infantry.
  • The howitzers. Wikipedia gives the battery six, "five remaining" after one was lost. Appleman says the sixth was left at P'yongt'aek with a broken prime mover, so five were at Osan; he also says several reports wrongly had all of them destroyed. The game gives six.
  • The tanks hit. Appleman counts four destroyed or immobilised and three damaged; Wikipedia's summary, one destroyed and three disabled.
  • The North Korean infantry. Wikipedia puts the column at nearly 5,000 men; Appleman says about 1,000 got off the trucks and deployed in front of the ridge.
  • The American losses. Smith reckoned about 150 of the infantry, 155 by one estimate; the division's first report said 148 men and 5 officers missing. On 7 July 5 officers and 26 men of the artillery were still missing. Wikipedia gives a later count of 60 dead, 21 wounded and 82 captured, of whom 32 died in captivity. Wikipedia's Korean War, after Stokesbury, gives 180 casualties. The Army's 2019 article says 150 killed or missing. Appleman counts 250 survivors by 6 July.
  • The North Korean losses. Appleman gives about 42 killed and 85 wounded, and warns that some of these may have been lost at P'yongt'aek the next day.
  • The wounded left behind. Appleman could not find the medical sergeant's name. Wikipedia says the litter cases were later found shot where they lay and the medic was never seen again. Appleman records 36 men under Second Lieutenant Jansen C. Cox captured on 6 July; Seoul radio claimed 72.

The man who stayed

When Smith ordered the withdrawal at about 14:30, some 25 to 30 of his wounded could not walk, and the trucks were far back, by the north edge of Osan. The litter cases had to be left. A medical sergeant offered to stay with them. Appleman, writing the Army's official history, tried and failed to find out who he was. Wikipedia's account says the wounded were later found shot on their litters, and the sergeant was never seen again. He has no name in the record, only the fact that he stayed.

How the field is drawn

Task Force Smith's position north of Osan, 5 July 1950, at 10 m a hex: 220 x 110 hexes, about 2200 m east to west and 950 m north to south, north at the top: the hill line across the middle, the highway over it at the saddle on the left, the railroad on the right, rice paddies before and behind. The hills, the saddle, the paddies and the line are drawn by hand to the shape the accounts give, not traced from any map; the deployment is the infantry attack near noon, in our own words, with round numbers for play. A wet morning after rain; the paddies are deep in water. There are no vehicle rules: the T-34s are on call as tanks firing over open sights (Fire support), and the Americans' recoilless rifles and bazookas fight as riflemen. Their foxholes are men gone to ground: they start that way. Most of the force were young soldiers new to battle (green).

From exchange Phase What happens

Fox Hill at Toktong Pass, 27-28 November 1950

  • The armies: United Nations and Chinese.
  • Fought for: the crest Fox Company held, attacked by the Chinese.
  • The field: 150 by 120 hexes of 10 m, about 1,500 by 1,040 m, north at the top.
  • The weather: Fair, strong wind from the north-west, night.
  • Wounds: Korea 1950-53 - hospitalized wounded.
  • On the travel map: Chosin Reservoir, 1950 (Yudam-ni to Hungnam), at Toktong Pass (Fox Hill).

The campaign

After the Inchon landing and the breakout from the Pusan perimeter in September 1950, the United Nations armies went north to unite Korea before the year was out. The mountains split them. The Eighth Army went up the west side; X Corps, under Major General Edward Almond, and the South Korean I Corps went up the east. The 1st Marine Division, under Major General Oliver P. Smith, landed at Wonsan with X Corps and was sent inland up a single mountain road towards the Chosin (Changjin) Reservoir.

China had given warnings. The Chinese People's Volunteers began to cross the Yalu on 19 October, about 200,000 men, and opened their First Phase Offensive on 25 October. On 2 November the Marines met the Chinese 124th Division, which then drew back north. The 9th Army Group under Song Shilun (Sung Shih-lun to Simmons; Wikipedia calls it the 9th Corps) reached the reservoir about 17 November, with the 20th, 26th and 27th Armies, 11 or 12 divisions. Smith warned General Cates privately that his division could end up strung out along one mountain road. On 25 November, as the Chinese struck the Eighth Army on the Ch'ongch'on River, X Corps ordered the Marines west from Yudam-ni as the northern arm of a pincer.

On 27 November the 5th and 7th Marines were at Yudam-ni, the division base at Hagaru-ri to the south-east. Between them the road climbed through Toktong Pass. The 7th Marines ordered Captain William E. Barber's Fox Company, 2nd Battalion, 7th Marines, to hold the pass. It left Hagaru-ri at 15:00 in trucks lent by H Battery, 11th Marines, and arrived at 17:00. With sections of water-cooled machine guns and 81 mm mortars from the battalion's Weapons Company it was 240 officers and men, by Simmons' count. That night the 9th Army Group attacked all along the road. The 79th and 89th Divisions went for Yudam-ni; the 59th Division went round to cut the road at the pass. At Yudam-ni the thermometer fell to -20°F (about -29°C).

The places

  • Yudam-ni: the village west of the reservoir where the 5th and 7th Marines were attacked on 27 November.
  • Hagaru-ri: the division base at the south end of the reservoir, with its howitzers and an airstrip that opened on 1 December.
  • Toktong Pass: the pass on the road between them. Fox Company was to keep three miles of road open, starting four miles out of Hagaru-ri.
  • Fox Hill: the hill at the middle of the pass, north of the road; one Marine called it a saddle-like hill to the right of the road. The 3rd Platoon held its crest.
  • The road: below the hill to the south, where the headquarters and service platoon lay. The corpsmen used a Korean hut as a sick bay.
  • The high hill to the north: the ground above Fox Hill from which the Chinese fired machine guns on 1 December.
  • The valley to the south: across the road, from which the Chinese attacked on 30 November.
  • Hill 1419: a height south of Yudam-ni, where C Company, 1st Battalion, 7th Marines was attacked on 28 November and which the 1st Battalion took on 1 December on its way to Fox Hill.

The leaders

  • William E. Barber (American, Fox Company): an Iwo Jima veteran, he had taken command on 7 November. He was wounded on the second night and went on commanding.
  • Robert C. McCarthy (American, 3rd Platoon): held the crest, and lost most of his forward squads in the first attack.
  • Elmo G. Peterson and John M. Dunne (American, 2nd and 1st Platoons): held the west and east sides of the perimeter.
  • Raymond G. Davis (American, 1st Battalion, 7th Marines): led the march over the mountains that reached Fox Hill on 2 December. He received the Medal of Honor.
  • Litzenberg (American, 7th Marines): the regimental commander, who sent Fox Company to the pass.
  • Randolph S. D. Lockwood (American, 2nd Battalion, 7th Marines): Fox Company's battalion commander, at Hagaru-ri; his attempt to reach the pass got nowhere.
  • Oliver P. Smith (American, 1st Marine Division): his aide-memoire is the basis of Rasula's account.
  • Song Shilun (Chinese, 9th Army Group): commanded the Chinese attack at the reservoir.
  • 59th Division (Chinese, 20th Army): the division that attacked Fox Hill. No source read for this page names its commander or the regiments engaged.

The battle

Times here are local, as the Marine records give them; none of the sources read says which clock, but Korea's standard time was GMT+9. McCarthy's 3rd Platoon held the crest, Peterson's 2nd Platoon the left and Dunne's 1st Platoon the right, with headquarters near the road. At about 02:30 on 28 November the Chinese attacked from several sides at once. A company-sized attack overran McCarthy's two forward squads: of 35 men, 15 were killed, 9 wounded and 3 missing, and 8 fell back. The wing platoons held. Simmons credits much of this to three men: Private Hector A. Cafferata and a Private First Class Benson of the 2nd Platoon, and Private First Class Gerald J. Smith of the 1st. The Chinese reached the company's mortars, and the fighting was hand to hand until dawn. By 06:30 they had been driven off. Fox Company had lost 20 killed, 54 wounded and 3 missing. Rasula's account counts about 450 Chinese dead.

On 28 November H Battery, 11th Marines at Hagaru-ri registered its howitzers on the ground round the hill. Australian F-51 Mustangs made a strike for the company, and Marine R5D transports dropped medical supplies and mortar bombs; fetching the drops cost two more wounded. Ordered to break out towards C Company, 1st Battalion, Fox Company could not move its 54 wounded. Davis's battalion fought its way out from Yudam-ni to C Company that day and was called back.

The second attack came from 02:15 to 06:00 on 29 November. Five Marines were killed and 29 wounded, among them Barber, hit in the leg. At 10:30 a helicopter bringing radio batteries was hit by small-arms fire and left without taking out any wounded. That afternoon Flying Boxcars of the Combat Cargo Command dropped supplies some 600 yards off target. At 02:30 on 30 November the Chinese attacked again from across the valley to the south and were stopped by the machine guns and mortars. A second battery helicopter was hit at 14:30, and an evening drop landed up to 800 yards away. At 01:00 on 1 December the Chinese set up four machine guns on the high hill to the north; the artillery, aimed by the light of 81 mm illuminating rounds, knocked them out. Marine aircraft struck the hill at 10:30.

On 1 December Davis's 1st Battalion took Hill 1419. Wikipedia says the 59th Division put in its last five platoons against it. After dark the battalion set out across the mountains east of the road, over three ridges, in deep snow and a snowstorm, about 8 miles by Davis's citation. It made radio contact with Fox Company at 06:30 on 2 December and reached its lines at 11:25. Rasula's totals for Fox Company are 26 killed, 3 missing and 89 wounded; six of its seven officers had been hit. Barber's citation says only 82 of his men could walk off the hill.

The wounded lay in the corpsmen's hut. One, Corporal Howard W. Koone, was told he was third on the list for a helicopter; it never came. Barber himself refused morphine. Across the campaign, Wikipedia says, morphine had to be thawed in a corpsman's mouth and plasma froze. Fox Company's wounded went out with Davis's column, which reached Hagaru-ri on 4 December with 22 litter cases and many walking wounded. By the caption of a Marine Corps photograph, 4,312 wounded and frostbitten men were flown out from the airstrip there, by C-47s among others, before the division went south.

Where the accounts disagree

  • When the first attack began. Simmons and Rasula say about 02:30. Armchair General's 2011 game article gives 02:07.
  • Fox Company's strength. Simmons gives 240 with the attachments; Rasula about 220 and a mortar section; Barber's citation 220; Wikipedia's article on Barber 246. The game uses 240.
  • The Chinese strength. Simmons calls the first attack company-sized; Rasula says two battalions; Barber's citation calls it of estimated regimental strength; Wikipedia's article on Barber says more than 1,400 men. The game uses about a company with others fed in.
  • The Chinese losses. Simmons says Fox Company never knew, with guesses up to 500 on the first night. Rasula counts 450 that night and probably more than 1,000 in all.
  • The first night's losses. Simmons gives 20 killed and 54 wounded; Rasula adds 3 missing; Wikipedia's article on Barber says 20 killed and 45 wounded.
  • Barber's wound. His citation says he was hit in the leg early on 29 November; Wikipedia's article says a ricochet lodged in his pelvis and broke the bone.
  • The relief. Rasula, Wikipedia and Davis's citation put it on the morning of 2 December; Armchair General says 1 December. Davis's citation has his battalion reach Hagaru-ri on the morning of 4 December; Wikipedia's article on Barber, on the night of 3-4 December.
  • Benson's name. Simmons calls him Private First Class Robert Benson. Cafferata's obituaries, as Wikipedia gives them, call him Kenneth Benson, later awarded the Silver Star.
  • The cold. Simmons gives -20°F at Yudam-ni on the night of 27 November. Wikipedia says temperatures in the campaign fell to about -36°F.
  • The photograph. The Marine Corps caption of the picture above dates the relief attempt 27 November; Fox Company was not cut off until early on 28 November, and Wikipedia puts the failed attempts on 29 November.

Without his boots

Private Hector Cafferata, a reservist called up in September 1950, was in the 2nd Platoon on the west side of Fox Hill. When the Chinese came on in the dark of 28 November, the rest of his fire team was hit. By the account in his obituaries he could not find his boots or coat, and fought for hours in the snow without them. Kenneth Benson, blinded for a time by a grenade, kept reloading his rifle. His citation credits him with 15 enemy killed. Later a grenade fell into a shallow trench holding wounded Marines. Cafferata "seized the deadly missile in his right hand" and threw it; it burst and took off part of a finger. A sniper then wounded him. He reached Japan in December and the Navy hospital at St Albans in January.

How the field is drawn

Fox Hill over Toktong Pass on the night of 27-28 November 1950, at 10 m a hex: 150 x 120 hexes, about 1500 m east to west and 1040 m north to south, north at the top: the hill Fox Company held in the middle, the road through the pass below it to the south, the heights to the north, a ridge across the road. The hill, road, rocks and slopes are drawn by hand to the shape the accounts give, not traced from any map; the deployment is the first night's attack, in our own words, with round numbers for play. Bitter cold (-20 F): automatic weapons jam, men move slowly; deep snow; a dark night with a strong wind from the north-west. Corsairs fly only by day.

The perimeter at Chipyong-ni, 14-15 February 1951

  • The armies: United Nations and Chinese.
  • Fought for: G Company's hill on the southern perimeter, attacked by the Chinese.
  • The field: 200 by 170 hexes of 10 m, about 2,000 by 1,470 m, north at the top.
  • The weather: Fair, breeze from the north-west, night.
  • Wounds: Korea 1950-53 - hospitalized wounded.
  • On the travel map: Chipyong-ni, 1951 (Yangpyong to Wonju), at Chipyong-ni.

The campaign

The Chinese People's Volunteers entered the war in November 1950 and drove the United Nations armies out of North Korea. On 23 December the Eighth Army's commander, General Walton Walker, was killed in a road accident, and Lieutenant General Matthew B. Ridgway took command on the 26th. The Chinese opened their third phase offensive on the evening of 31 December. Seoul was given up on 3 January 1951, and by about 7 January Peng Dehuai, the Chinese commander, had halted his worn-out troops.

Ridgway then went back onto the attack with Operations Thunderbolt and Roundup. Colonel Paul L. Freeman's 23rd Regimental Combat Team, of the 2nd Infantry Division, beat off a Chinese attack at the Twin Tunnels at the start of February and reached Chipyong-ni on 3 February. On the night of 11 February the Chinese opened their fourth phase offensive. The XIII Army Group struck X Corps at Hoengsong; the ROK 8th Division was broken, with 323 officers and 7,142 men dead or missing. X Corps fell back to a line anchored on Chipyong-ni and Wonju, and the 23rd was left out on a limb.

On 13 February Lieutenant General Edward Almond, of X Corps, decided to pull the 23rd back about 15 miles to Yoju. After meeting MacArthur at Suwon that noon, Ridgway judged that giving up Chipyong-ni would open the Han valley, and ordered it held. The roads behind the regiment were already being cut.

The places

  • Chipyong-ni: a crossroads town on Route 24 and a single-track railway, about 40 miles east of Seoul.
  • The perimeter: a ring about a mile across on the low ground round the town. Freeman left the higher hills outside it, which would have needed a line about 12 miles long.
  • Hill 397 (Mangmi-san): the height a mile south of the town that overlooked it, from which the Chinese came at G Company.
  • G Company's hill: the southern edge of the perimeter, held by the 2nd Battalion, where the Chinese broke in on 15 February.
  • Pongmi-san and the other hills: Pongmi-san to the north-east, and Hills 248, 345, 348, 506 and 319, all outside the perimeter.
  • Route 24A and Koksu-ri: the road south to Yoju, blocked at Koksu-ri on 12 February, by which Task Force Crombez came.
  • The road cut: a deep cutting on the western slopes of Hill 397, a mile below the town, where the relief column was hit.

The leaders

  • Paul L. Freeman (UN, 23rd Infantry): chose the tight perimeter. Wounded in the leg by a mortar fragment on the first night, he refused to be taken out and kept command until the morning of 15 February.
  • Raoul Magrin-Vernerey, "Monclar" (UN, French Battalion): 58, a former général de corps d'armée who took the rank of lieutenant-colonel to lead the battalion, which held the west side.
  • James W. Edwards (UN, 2nd Battalion, 23rd Infantry): held the south and led the counter-attacks for G Company's hill.
  • John H. Chiles (UN, X Corps G-3): flown in on 14 February to take over; he took command when Freeman went out.
  • Matthew B. Ridgway (UN, Eighth Army): overruled Almond and ordered the town held.
  • Marcel G. Crombez (UN, 5th Cavalry): sent his tanks ahead when the infantry could not get through in time.
  • Edgar J. Treacy (UN, 3rd Battalion, 5th Cavalry): rode with the column, was left behind at Koksu-ri and taken prisoner; he died in captivity.
  • Xu Guofu (Chinese, 119th Division): the field commander at Chipyong-ni, whose memoirs give the Chinese account.
  • Wen Yucheng (Chinese, 40th Army): ordered the withdrawal when it was learned that the garrison was much larger than thought.

The battle

The sources do not say which clock they keep; the times here are taken as local. Freeman had about 4,500 men: the 23rd Infantry, the French Battalion, the 1st Ranger Company, the 37th Field Artillery Battalion, a battery of 155 mm howitzers, anti-aircraft guns of the 82nd AAA Battalion and B Company of the 2nd Engineers. The 1st Battalion held the north, the 3rd the east, the 2nd the south and the French the west. B Company and the Rangers were the reserve.

At about 22:00 on 13 February machine guns and mortars opened on C Company, astride Route 24. At about 23:30 the Chinese attacked C Company, then G Company in the south, the French and the 3rd Battalion. They got into G Company's line once, but F Company and the tank company threw them out. Attacks at 06:30 on the 3rd Battalion and an hour later on the French failed, and the Chinese drew back into the hills. About 100 of Freeman's men had been hit.

On 14 February wind and mortar fire stopped the helicopters taking out the wounded. From about 15:00 two dozen C-119s dropped supplies for three hours. Near midnight a barrage of about an hour fell on the command post. A heavy assault from Hill 397 struck G Company, then A and C Companies in the north and I and K in the east. I Company's line was broken once and restored. In the south the pressure did not stop, and at about 03:00 on the 15th G Company gave up the rest of its hill. The gunners of B Battery, 503rd, fell back with it, leaving their 155 mm howitzers between the lines.

At about 04:00 Edwards sent in a platoon of F Company and a platoon of Rangers with G Company's survivors. They took back part of the hill and were driven off. At 10:00 B Company attacked alone behind mortar, tank and anti-aircraft fire and was kept off the crest. From noon fighter-bombers struck the Chinese on the southern slopes. At about 16:30 B Company took the rest of the hill.

Crombez had come up from Yoju with the 5th Cavalry, but saw that his infantry could not reach the town by dark. At 15:45 he left them and drove on with 23 tanks, of D Company, 6th Tank Battalion, and a platoon of A Company, 70th Tank Battalion, with about 160 men of L Company, 5th Cavalry, riding on the decks. At the halts near Koksu-ri the tanks moved off before all the riders were back on, and about 90 were left behind. In the road cut the Chinese fired rockets and threw satchel charges; a rocket hit Captain Johnnie M. Hiers's tank and killed him and the turret crew, but the burned driver took it through. Crombez entered the perimeter at about 17:15, and the Chinese on Hill 397 ran. Of L Company, 23 men were left with the column, 13 of them wounded.

The wounded of the 23rd lay inside the perimeter, with a platoon of the 2nd Medical Battalion, until the road opened. On 16 February fog and snow grounded the helicopters again; a supply train of 28 lorries and 19 ambulances came up from the south, and the wounded went out to the 5th Cavalry's clearing station at Koksu-ri before dark.

Where the accounts disagree

  • The garrison. Mossman and Gugeler give about 4,500 men, of them 2,500 front-line infantry. Wikipedia, after Xu, says the Chinese expected about 1,000 and found over 6,000. The military.com account puts the French at about 800, 180 of them South Koreans.
  • The Chinese strength. Wikipedia gives a US estimate of 25,000 and counts eight regiments, about 8,000 men, in the area. Mossman's prisoners named six regiments in the attacks, from the 115th, 116th, 119th, 120th and 126th Divisions of the 39th, 40th and 42nd Armies. Xu says only three regiments, the 356th, 357th and 359th, about 3,000 men, attacked; two more, the 343rd and 376th, lost their way.
  • The UN losses. Mossman gives 52 killed, 259 wounded and 42 missing. Wikipedia gives 51 killed and 250 wounded. A 2009 Army article adds 51 non-battle casualties.
  • The Chinese losses. Mossman has the 23rd count and estimate 4,946 Chinese casualties, and Crombez over 500 more. Wikipedia, after US sources, gives about 2,000 killed and 3,000 wounded. Xu admits "a little over 900" casualties, a third of them dead. The 2009 Army article claims over 7,000 counted dead.
  • The counter-attacks. Mossman has Edwards's composite force attack at about 04:00 and B Company at 10:00. Wikipedia, after Gugeler, has the Rangers, an F Company platoon and 14 men of G Company driven back at 06:15, and B Company attacking at noon.
  • Crombez's arrival. Mossman says about 17:15, Gugeler 17:00, Wikipedia 17:25 and military.com 17:10. Military.com has the column leave at 15:00, the others at 15:45. Wikipedia says nearly 20 tanks arrived; the captured Chinese XIX Army Group critique, as Ryan gives it, says more than 20, at about 16:00.
  • L Company's loss. Mossman and Gugeler give 12 killed, about 40 wounded and 19 missing. Military.com says more than 130 riders were killed, wounded, captured or stranded.
  • Hill 397. Mossman puts it south of the town; Wikipedia says north. The accounts of the fighting agree with Mossman.

Sergeant Sitman's grenade

Sergeant First Class William S. Sitman, of Pennsylvania, led a machine-gun section of M Company, 23rd Infantry, attached to I Company on the eastern side of the perimeter. On the night of 14 February the Chinese came at his position. A grenade put his own gun out of action, and he stayed on to protect the crew of a light machine gun that had moved in. When a grenade landed among them, his Medal of Honor citation says, he threw himself on it, "absorbing the full force of the explosion with his body." He died of his wounds. Five men lived. He was 27.

How the field is drawn

The perimeter at Chipyong-ni on the night of 14-15 February 1951, at 10 m a hex: 200 x 170 hexes, about 2000 m east to west and 1470 m north to south, north at the top: the village in the middle, the railroad through its south, the road north and south, and the ring of low hills the 23rd Infantry dug in on, about a mile across. The hills, the village, the railroad and the paddies are drawn by hand to the shape the accounts give, not traced from any map; the deployment is the second night's attack, in our own words, with round numbers for play. A clear, bitter night with snow on the ground and the paddies frozen hard (open ground). It is dark: fire the illumination (the transports' flares) or flares from the line to see what is coming. The fighter-bombers fly only by day.

The phases

From exchange Phase What happens
1 The attack on G Company Soon after 22:00 on 14 February the Chinese regiment from Hill 397 breaks into G Company's line.
331 G Company's hill falls; first reserves About 03:00 G Company gives up the rest of its hill; a Ranger platoon and an F Company platoon reach it and counter-attack in the dark.
496 The dawn counter-attack fails 06:15: the counter-attack by the Rangers, F Company's platoon and G Company's survivors is driven back.
721 B Company counter-attacks 10:00: behind a mortar barrage and tank fire, B Company attacks G Company's hill; it is kept off the crest for hours (Mossman).
1111 The hill retaken; the Chinese run About 16:30 B Company regains the rest of the hill as tanks appear on Route 24A; the Chinese on Hill 397 begin to run.
1156 Task Force Crombez About 17:15: Crombez leads his tanks inside the perimeter (Mossman).

Hill 504 and the valley at Kapyong, 23-24 April 1951

  • The armies: United Nations and Chinese.
  • Fought for: Hill 504's summit, attacked by the Chinese.
  • The field: 220 by 160 hexes of 10 m, about 2,200 by 1,390 m, north at the top.
  • The weather: Fair, calm or light air, night.
  • Wounds: Korea 1950-53 - hospitalized wounded.
  • On the travel map: Kapyong, 1951 (the Kapyong valley), at Hill 504.
  • The record: the fight lasted about 871 exchanges (a minute each).

The campaign

By April 1951 Ridgway's offensives had pushed the Chinese and North Koreans back across the 38th parallel. On 22 April Peng Dehuai opened the Chinese Spring Offensive, the first stage of the fifth phase campaign. It aimed to destroy the US I and IX Corps north of the Han and take Seoul. The 39th and 40th Armies were put under Song Shilun's 9th Army Group. Wen Yucheng, of the 40th Army, was given the task of destroying the ROK 6th Division and blocking the Kapyong valley against help.

The ROK 6th Division, under Major General Chang Do Yong, had stopped at 16:00 on 22 April to dig in. The 118th and 60th Divisions struck at 17:00 and slipped through the gaps, and by 23:00 Chang had lost touch with his regiments. The division broke, rallied and broke again, and its men streamed south down the Kapyong valley.

The 27th British Commonwealth Infantry Brigade was in IX Corps reserve near Kapyong. Brigadier Basil Coad had gone to Hong Kong on 23 March, and Brigadier Brian Burke commanded. The 1st Argyll and Sutherland Highlanders had already left for Pusan, so Burke had three battalions: the 3rd Battalion, Royal Australian Regiment (Lieutenant Colonel Bruce Ferguson), the 2nd Battalion, Princess Patricia's Canadian Light Infantry (Lieutenant Colonel James Stone), and the 1st Battalion, Middlesex Regiment. With them were the 16th Field Regiment, Royal New Zealand Artillery, with 25-pounders; A Company of the US 72nd Heavy Tank Battalion with 15 Shermans; and two companies of the 2nd Chemical Mortar Battalion. On 23 April the brigade was sent forward to block the valley.

The places

  • The Kapyong valley: where a tributary joins the Kapyong River, less than 3 km wide at its widest by Veterans Affairs Canada's reckoning (the Australian War Memorial says 7 km), and about 30 km south of the front.
  • Hill 504: the height east of the river held by 3 RAR. D Company held the summit, A Company the north-west spur and C Company a rear spur.
  • B Company's knoll: a small hill by the river and road, below Hill 504.
  • Hill 677: the height west of the river held by 2 PPCLI.
  • Sudok San (Hill 794): a height between the two battalions, left undefended.
  • Chuktun-ni: the hamlet in the valley behind Hill 504, where 3 RAR's headquarters stood.
  • The ford: where 3 RAR crossed the Kapyong River on the evening of 24 April to reach the Middlesex.
  • Kapyong: the town to the south, on the road to Seoul.

The leaders

  • Brian Burke (UN, 27th British Commonwealth Infantry Brigade): ordered the Australians out on 24 April and told the Canadians by loudspeaker that they were on their own.
  • Bruce Ferguson (UN, 3 RAR): withdrew his headquarters before dawn on 24 April and directed the battalion from the rear. He received the DSO.
  • Ben O'Dowd (UN, A Company, 3 RAR): held the north-west spur and was left in charge on the hill.
  • Reg Saunders (UN, C Company, 3 RAR): his company stood ready to reinforce A and B Companies.
  • James Stone (UN, 2 PPCLI): refused to give up Hill 677 and held his fire on the attack on his headquarters until it was 40 m off.
  • Michael Levy (UN, 10 Platoon, 2 PPCLI): when his platoon was nearly overrun, his request for gunfire on his own position went back through Captain J. G. W. Mills.
  • Kenneth W. Koch (UN, A Company, 72nd Heavy Tank Battalion): his Shermans fought in the valley, carried supplies up and took out wounded.
  • Chang Do Yong (ROK, 6th Division): his division's collapse opened the valley.
  • Wen Yucheng (Chinese, 40th Army): charged with the drive down the valley.
  • Deng Yue (Chinese, 118th Division): Wikipedia names him over the 118th and 60th Divisions, together perhaps 20,000 men.

The battle

The sources do not say which clock they keep; the times here are taken as local. From about 20:00 on 23 April South Korean soldiers came back through the brigade, mostly through 3 RAR, with Chinese among them. At 21:30 the Chinese struck the forward platoon of tanks by the road; two tank commanders, fighting from open turrets, were killed, and the tanks fell back. At about 22:00 the 354th Regiment of the 118th Division reached 3 RAR. Two battalions went for A and B Companies. The third worked round the Australian left and reached the headquarters at Chuktun-ni. The 16th Field Regiment pulled back about 4 miles at about 03:00, and the 2nd Chemical Mortar Battalion's company with 3 RAR left its mortars and walked away before midnight.

A Company's 1 Platoon was attacked from 21:30, and its survivors fell back at about 01:00. At 00:50 the Chinese struck B Company's 4 Platoon and were beaten off after an hour; at 03:30 they broke into 6 Platoon and were thrown out with the tanks' help; a last attack at 04:45 failed. Between 05:00 and 06:00 Ferguson took his headquarters back down the valley, the Shermans escorting it. At dawn O'Dowd's 3 Platoon took back the lost position.

At 07:15 B Company was ordered off its knoll to join the rest of the battalion; at 09:30, the order rescinded, it went back, and Lieutenant Leonard Montgomerie's 4 Platoon took the knoll again with the bayonet. On the summit D Company's 12 Platoon beat off six attacks between 07:00 and 10:30, and more until 13:30. The Shermans brought food, water and ammunition up and took the wounded out. After 15:00 American Corsairs dropped napalm on D Company in error and killed two men.

At 14:30 Burke's order to withdraw was given out. The barrage meant to cover it was late, and the tanks fired over open sights instead. C Company went at 16:30 and A Company followed, down a ridge to the ford; D Company broke clean after dark. B Company carried the wounded, and Chinese prisoners were made to carry stretchers. 3 RAR passed through the Middlesex that evening.

At 22:00 on 24 April the Chinese turned on 2 PPCLI. Private Wayne Mitchell, wounded, charged them three times with his Bren gun. About 500 Chinese came at Stone's headquarters; he held fire until they were 40 m off, then opened with his half-tracks and mortars. At 01:10 on the 25th D Company's 10 Platoon was nearly overrun, and Mills asked for gunfire on his own position. The New Zealand guns fired on it while the men lay in their trenches. At dawn the attacks stopped. The battalion was short of food and ammunition. At 14:00 Canadian patrols found the road behind them open.

Where the accounts disagree

  • The Chinese. Mossman and Wikipedia name the 118th Division of the 40th Army and the 60th Division of the 20th Army. The Anzac Portal says the 19th Chinese Corps broke the ROK 6th Division, and gives 2,800 UN troops against the 118th Division's 10,600.
  • The scale of the offensive. Wikipedia gives over 700,000 men in all, 337,000 in the western thrust. McGibbon says about 270,000 were set in motion.
  • The Australian losses. Wikipedia and The Canadian Encyclopedia give 32 killed and 59 wounded; the Australian War Memorial 32 and 53; the Anzac Portal 32 killed, more than 50 wounded and 3 taken prisoner. Mossman gives 31 killed, 58 wounded and 3 missing.
  • The Canadian losses. Veterans Affairs Canada, The Canadian Encyclopedia and Mossman give 10 killed and 23 wounded; Wikipedia gives 18 and 38.
  • The Chinese losses. The Anzac Portal says over 2,000 lost to the Australians and Canadians; The Canadian Encyclopedia about 2,000 killed and wounded. Wikipedia's infobox gives about 6,000 killed, and cites Bjarnason for 4,000 killed by the New Zealand guns alone.
  • The gunfire on 10 Platoon. The Canadian Encyclopedia says 2,300 rounds in under an hour. Wikipedia describes barrages of 15 to 20 minutes each.
  • The airdrop. Mossman says C-119s from Japan dropped supplies about six hours after Stone asked. Wikipedia says no resupply reached the battalion. A veteran told Veterans Affairs Canada that some supplies were dropped.
  • The order of the withdrawal. Wikipedia has C Company go first at 16:30, then A Company. The Memorial's anniversary blog says B Company left first, up Hill 504 and down the ridge.
  • When 3 RAR got clear. The Anzac Portal has it inside the Middlesex lines at 19:30; Mossman shortly after dark; Wikipedia says 23:30.
  • Who flanked the headquarters. The Anzac Portal has the 354th's third battalion go round the Australian left. Our game brings it round the east of the hill.
  • O'Dowd's rank. The Memorial's exhibition calls him Major; its anniversary blog, Captain.

The signaller from Cronulla

Private Horace "Bill" Madden was a signaller at 3 RAR's headquarters. Laying telephone line on 24 April, he was knocked out by a grenade, and later thrown into a weapon pit by another blast. He was taken in the withdrawal with Privates Robert Parker and Keith Gwyther, concussed. As a prisoner he would not cooperate. He was beaten, had ribs broken with a rifle butt, and was starved, yet shared the food he could buy with sick men. He died of malnutrition and ill-treatment in November 1951, aged 27, the only Australian to die in Chinese hands. He was given the George Cross after his death. The Anzac Portal gives his death as 9 November; Wikipedia, about the 6th.

Hill 931 on Heartbreak Ridge, October 1951

  • The armies: United Nations and North Koreans.
  • Fought for: Hill 931, attacked by the United Nations.
  • The field: 170 by 260 hexes of 10 m, about 1,700 by 2,250 m, north at the top.
  • The weather: Fair, breeze from the north-west.
  • Wounds: Korea 1950-53 - hospitalized wounded.
  • On the travel map: Heartbreak Ridge, 1951 (the Mundung-ni and Sat'ae-ri valleys), at Hill 931.
  • The record: the fight lasted about 901 exchanges (a minute each).

The campaign

Armistice talks opened at Kaesong in July 1951. The front stayed still while they went on, but neither side stopped fighting. Hermes says the Communist delegates called off the meetings on the night of 22 August, and early on the 23rd they said a UN aircraft had bombed the conference site. The UN investigators did not believe it, and Ridgway thought the break had been planned in advance.

In the east, X Corps under Major General Clovis E. Byers held the line round the Punchbowl. The 2nd Infantry Division attacked Bloody Ridge from 18 August. The ROK 36th Regiment took it and was driven off. Attacks by the US 9th Infantry failed, and the ridge fell only when the 23rd and 38th Infantry worked round both flanks. The North Koreans left on 4 and 5 September, leaving more than 500 dead on the heights. On 5 September Van Fleet dropped a larger offensive in favour of limited attacks to tidy up the line.

The North Koreans dug in again about 1,500 yards north, on a hill mass some 7 miles long. Its peaks were Hill 894 in the south, Hill 931, about 1,300 yards beyond it and the highest, and Hill 851, about 2,100 yards further north. The press came to call it Heartbreak Ridge. Korea's veterans' ministry says the name came from a UPI reporter, Stan Carter, after he saw a wounded soldier at an aid station.

The places

  • Hill 931: the highest peak and the 23rd Infantry's objective, taken and lost several times in September.
  • Hill 894: the southern peak, taken by the 2nd Battalion, 9th Infantry, on 15 September.
  • Hill 851: the northern peak, the last taken, on 13 October.
  • Hill 520: a small hump at the western tip of a spur off the crest, taken by G Company, 2nd Battalion, 23rd Infantry, on 10 October.
  • The Sat'ae-ri valley: east of the ridge, up which the 23rd first attacked.
  • The Mundung-ni valley: west of the ridge, up which the tanks went from 10 October.
  • Bloody Ridge: to the south, fought over from 18 August to 5 September.
  • The Punchbowl: the round valley nearby; the battle took the sag out of X Corps' line there.
  • Panmunjom: where the talks began again on 25 October 1951.

The leaders

  • Clovis E. Byers (UN, X Corps): gave Hill 931 first priority, and with Young called off the September attacks.
  • Thomas E. de Shazo (UN, 2nd Division, acting): sent in the 23rd Infantry on 13 September. Wikipedia spells him Deshazo.
  • Robert N. Young (UN, 2nd Division): took command on 20 September and later called the first attacks a "fiasco" (Hermes).
  • James Y. Adams (UN, 23rd Infantry): told Young on 26 September it was "suicide" to keep to the plan.
  • Henry F. Daniels and Virgil E. Craven (UN, 2nd and 3rd Battalions, 23rd Infantry): led the night attack of 5 October.
  • Ralph Monclar (UN, French Battalion): the name taken by Raoul Magrin-Vernerey, a general who stepped down to lieutenant-colonel to lead the battalion.
  • John O. Woods (UN, 72nd Tank Battalion): led the tanks up the Mundung-ni valley.
  • Robert W. Love (UN, 2nd Engineer Combat Battalion): built the road the tanks used.
  • Hong Nim (North Korean, 6th Division): sent the fresh 13th Regiment onto the ridge in mid-September (Hermes).

The battle

The sources give hours without naming a clock; the times here are taken as local. At 05:30 on 13 September a 30-minute bombardment began, and the 23rd Infantry went up from the east, Craven's 3rd Battalion leading and Daniels's 2nd behind. Hidden bunkers held by the 1st Regiment of the North Korean 6th Division stopped them at the foot of the spur by nightfall. The 2nd Battalion, 9th Infantry, took Hill 894 on the 15th and lost over 200 men to counter-attacks in the next two days. Through the rest of the month the 23rd attacked 931 again and again. Its men reached the crest on 23 September, but the 3rd Regiment of the 12th Division threw them off. On 26 September the French Battalion and the 23rd failed against the 15th Regiment. On the 27th Young and Byers stopped the attacks. The 23rd had lost over 950 men.

Hermes says North Korean mortars caused about 85 per cent of the division's casualties up to then. Korean civilian porters often dropped their loads and ran when the enemy came close, so riflemen had to carry the supplies and litters. Bringing a litter case down from the 23rd's forward positions could take up to ten hours. No source read for this page says how many of the ridge's wounded went out by helicopter; across the war, Zimmerman says, helicopters carried more than 20,000 casualties to the surgical hospitals.

Young's new plan, Operation Touchdown, was issued on 2 October. The whole division would attack together, and Love's engineers cleared a road up the Mundung-ni valley for the Shermans, blasting the roadblocks and mines by hand while the bulldozers were under repair. A small task force raided up the Sat'ae-ri valley on 3 and 4 October to draw attention there. Artillery and Marine Corsairs began the preparation in the late afternoon of 5 October, and the attack went in at 21:00. Hermes says the North Korean regiments facing it were all far under strength. By 03:00 on the 6th the 2nd and 3rd Battalions of the 23rd held the southern half of Hill 931. They beat off a counter-attack, and before noon they and the French had the whole hill.

On 10 October the 72nd Tank Battalion, with L Company of the 38th Infantry and a platoon of engineers, drove up the valley to Mundung-ni. It caught the Chinese 204th Division, of the 68th Army, in the open as it came in to relieve the North Koreans, and cut its supply routes. The same day G Company of the 2nd Battalion, 23rd, took Hill 520. Gugeler's account says it had about 20 men a platoon; it took three hours and over 30 casualties, mostly light grenade wounds, and flame throwers were brought up to clear the bunkers. The 1st Battalion and the French then worked north from bunker to bunker, and at daybreak on 13 October the French took Hill 851. The 38th Infantry took its last objective, Hill 1220, on 15 October.

Where the accounts disagree

  • The American loss. Hermes, as transcribed online, gives the 2nd Division over 3,800 casualties from 13 September to 15 October, almost half of them in the 23rd Infantry and the French. Wikipedia, citing Hermes, says over 3,700.
  • The enemy loss. The 2nd Division estimated about 25,000 North Korean and Chinese casualties, about half in Touchdown. Wikipedia calls this a US claim. No North Korean or Chinese figure was found for this page.
  • The French loss. The French ministry's Chemins de mémoire gives 60 killed and nearly 260 wounded; Wikipedia's article on the battalion, 60 and 200.
  • When it began. Hermes and Wikipedia start the battle on 13 September. Chemins de mémoire says the first attacks were on 15 September and the French were engaged from the 26th.
  • The mortar rounds. Hermes, as transcribed online, gives over 19,000 mortar rounds; Wikipedia gives over 119,000. The online text may have lost a figure.
  • Bloody Ridge. Hermes gives over 2,800 UN and ROK casualties there; Wikipedia, over 2,700.
  • The defenders. Wikipedia names Pang Ho San among the North Korean commanders without saying his post. Hermes names Hong Nim as commander of the 6th Division.

Company C on 931

Private First Class Herbert K. Pililaau was a Native Hawaiian from Waianae, Oahu, the ninth of 14 children and a singer and ukulele player. On 17 September 1951 his platoon of C Company, 23rd Infantry, was holding a position on the slope of Hill 931 when it was ordered to pull back. He stayed behind with his squad leader to cover it. He fired his Browning Automatic Rifle until it was empty, threw his grenades, and then fought with a trench knife and his fists until he was killed. When the position was retaken, more than 40 enemy dead lay round it. He was the first Hawaiian to receive the Medal of Honor.

How the field is drawn

Hill 931 on Heartbreak Ridge, October 1951, at 10 m a hex: 170 x 260 hexes, about 1700 m east to west and 2250 m north to south, north at the top: the narrow crest running north and south up the middle, Hill 931 in the upper part, Hill 894 at the bottom, spurs off both sides, the Mundung-ni valley along the west edge. The ridge, spurs, valley and bunkers are drawn by hand to the shape the accounts give, not traced from any map; the deployment is the October attack, in our own words, with round numbers for play. Steep slopes of shattered trees and rock; the North Koreans' bunkers on the crest; tanks in the valley (vehicles). A fair autumn day.

The armies as drawn up
