Pork Chop Hill, 16-17 April 1953

  • The armies: United Nations and Chinese.
  • Fought for: the top of Pork Chop Hill, attacked by the Chinese.
  • The field: 160 by 130 hexes of 10 m, about 1,600 by 1,130 m, north at the top.
  • The weather: Fair, calm or light air, night.
  • Wounds: Korea 1950-53 - hospitalized wounded.
  • On the travel map: Pork Chop Hill, 1953 (the outpost line north of Yeoncheon), at Pork Chop Hill.
  • The record: the fight lasted about 1496 exchanges (a minute each).

The campaign

By the end of 1952 the front had hardly moved for a year. The talks at Panmunjom were in a long recess, stuck on the exchange of prisoners. Both sides lived in deep bunkers and fought with raids, patrols and night attacks on the outposts in front of their main lines. Each outpost was a hill held by a company or a platoon. Hill 255, known as Porkchop, was one of them. Hermes says two platoons of I Company, 180th Infantry, took it on 6 June 1952, and that it was attacked twice in November. From the end of December it lay in the sector of the 7th Infantry Division, under Major General Arthur G. Trudeau.

On 23 March 1953 a battalion of the 423rd Regiment, 141st Division, of the Chinese 47th Army struck Old Baldy, Hill 266, while the Colombian Battalion was relieving its garrison. Two companies of the 201st Regiment, 67th Division, 23rd Army, struck Porkchop. Lieutenant Forrest Crittenden's company held it until its ammunition ran low and then pulled back from the crest, and the 31st Infantry took it again on the 24th. Old Baldy was not retaken; on 30 March General Taylor decided it was not essential. Pork Chop now stood with Chinese hills on three sides.

In April the talks moved again. The two sides agreed to exchange their sick and wounded prisoners, Operation Little Switch, from 20 April; the UN Command handed over 6,670 and received 684. Plenary sessions met again at Panmunjom on 26 April. Marino says the Chinese leaders wanted to show they would still fight, and that Deng Hua was allowed to attack before the exchange began.

The places

  • Pork Chop Hill (Hill 255): the outpost, ringed with trenches, bunkers and wire. Hermes spells it Porkchop.
  • Old Baldy (Hill 266): the neighbouring outpost, Outpost 11 to Pork Chop's Outpost 10 in Hermes, lost in March.
  • Hill 200: a smaller outpost close by, where part of L Company was held up.
  • The main line of resistance: the 7th Division's line on the hills to the south, from which the relief companies came.
  • Hasakkol: the Chinese-held ground from which Marino says the attacks came.
  • The chow bunker: a bunker on the hill where L Company's platoon was stopped about 50 yards short.
  • Panmunjom: where the talks went on through the fighting.

The leaders

  • Arthur G. Trudeau (UN, 7th Infantry Division): came forward by helicopter on 17 April and decided to hold the hill.
  • William B. Kern (UN, 31st Infantry): sent up the first reinforcements, and was then given the 1st and 2nd Battalions of the 17th Infantry.
  • John N. Davis (UN, battalion commander, 31st Infantry): his command post directed the fight.
  • Thomas Harrold (UN, E Company, 31st Infantry): held the hill when it was attacked. Wikipedia gives his middle initial as U., Marino as V.
  • Joseph G. Clemons (UN, K Company, 31st Infantry): a first lieutenant, West Point 1951, who led the counter-attack of 17 April.
  • Forrest Crittenden (UN, L Company, 31st Infantry): Wikipedia spells him Forest.
  • Walter B. Russell (UN, G Company, 17th Infantry): Clemons's brother-in-law, who came up to help him on the 17th.
  • Monroe D. King and Gorman C. Smith (UN, F and E Companies, 17th Infantry): came up on the night of 17 April.
  • Deng Hua (Chinese, commander in Korea): Wikipedia puts the 141st and 67th Divisions under him.
  • Hou Yung-chun (Chinese, 1st Battalion, 141st Division): named by Marino.

The battle

The accounts give hours without naming a clock; the times here are taken as local. On the night of 16 April 1953 E Company, 31st Infantry, held the hill with 96 men, of whom 76 were riflemen and 20 were out at listening posts. A patrol had gone out at 20:00. At about 23:00 Chinese infantry came up the slope out of the dark, and Harrold fired his signal flares. At about 23:05 the lights came on. A sergeant of E Company later recalled a flare, then artillery, mortars and bugles. The Chinese overran most of E Company's trenches.

At about 02:00 Kern sent reinforcements up. A platoon of F Company lost its way, and a platoon of L Company was stopped about 50 yards from the chow bunker. K Company, 135 men under Clemons, came forward, and at 04:30 the barrage lifted and it went up, with L Company attacking again. It took 29 minutes to cover 170 yards, and the first man reached the trenches at about 05:00. By 07:45 the company had gone about 200 yards in two hours. G Company of the 17th Infantry came up at 08:14 (Marino) and pulled out again at 15:00. At 11:00 Clemons radioed for water, plasma, litters, ammunition and flame throwers; little arrived but some water and rations.

Trudeau reached Davis's command post by helicopter at 15:00. At 16:40 Clemons reported about 20 men unhurt and asked to be relieved or withdrawn. Trudeau decided to hold, and with Eighth Army's leave put the 2nd Battalion, 17th Infantry, under the 31st. F Company of the 17th started up at 21:30; Chinese shelling killed 19 of its men on the way. K Company's survivors came off at about midnight. At 01:30 on 18 April the Chinese attacked again. E Company of the 17th came up and drove them back, and further attacks at 03:20 and 04:20 gained no ground. A Company of the 17th came up at dawn. The Chinese drew off at dusk on 18 April; the VFW account says by 18:00. The American guns fired tens of thousands of rounds a day, and Marshall says the Chinese fired almost as many (the figures are below).

The wounded lay in the trenches and bunkers for hours. K Company's medic, Sergeant Samuel K. Maxwell, used up his kit, and survivors went down between the Chinese salvos; some of K Company reached the foot of the hill in a weapons carrier. An engineer company, A Company of the 13th Engineer Battalion, was sent to dig out the trenches and ended up fighting as infantry.

The April battle is not the one fought there in July. On the night of 6 July 1953 the Chinese came again, in monsoon rain, with a battalion of the 200th Regiment, 67th Division, and later much of two divisions. Five American battalions made nine counter-attacks in four days, and on 11 July the hill was given up. The armistice was signed on 27 July.

Where the accounts disagree

  • The American loss. Wikipedia gives 104 killed and 373 wounded for April, without citing a source. K Company began with 135 men: Wikipedia says 125 were hit, 18 of them killed; Marino has 18 killed and 71 wounded by mid-afternoon on the 17th. An engineer told the VFW that only 11 men walked off of about 160 of K Company and 8 engineers.
  • The Chinese loss. No figure for April was found in the sources read for this page. Wikipedia lists it as unknown.
  • The Chinese units. Marino names the 141st Division and its 1st Battalion. Wikipedia names the 201st Regiment, which Hermes places in the 67th Division of the 23rd Army, as well as elements of the 141st.
  • The shells. Wikipedia says over 77,000 rounds were fired on the three outposts attacked, nearly 40,000 of them on Pork Chop on 18 April. Marino, after Marshall, gives 37,655 rounds on the first day and 77,349 on the second.
  • G Company's arrival. Marino gives 08:14; Wikipedia has it join K Company at 08:30.
  • How long it lasted. The VFW calls it a 45-hour battle; a West Point classmate's history, 48 hours; Wikipedia's opening says the Chinese broke contact after two days.
  • When the hill was first taken. Wikipedia says the 8th Cavalry first took it in October 1951 and the 180th Infantry retook it in May 1952. Hermes gives the 180th's capture as 6 June 1952.
  • The July losses. Wikipedia gives 243 Americans killed and 916 wounded in July, and a UN estimate of about 1,500 Chinese dead and 4,000 wounded; the Chinese army's medical history gives the 67th Division 533 killed and 1,242 wounded.

The medic of K Company

Sergeant Samuel K. Maxwell was K Company's medic when it went up Pork Chop before dawn on 17 April 1953. He recalled a Corporal Hatfield as the first man killed. Through the day he worked in the trenches with what he carried, until he had used every item in his kit. Clemons asked by radio for plasma and litters at 11:00, but almost none came. Later, when F Company of the 17th Infantry came up to relieve K Company, Maxwell gave what was left of his kit to one of its medics. Marino tells the story, and the VFW printed Maxwell's own recollections in 1995.

How the field is drawn

Pork Chop Hill on the night of 16-17 April 1953, at 10 m a hex: 160 x 130 hexes, about 1600 m east to west and 1130 m north to south, north at the top: Pork Chop in the middle, ringed with trenches and bunkers and wire, Hill 200 to the south-east, the main line's hills along the bottom, the valleys between cratered and wired. The hill, trenches, bunkers, valley and Hill 200 are drawn by hand to the shape the accounts give, not traced from any map; the deployment is the Chinese attack, in our own words, with round numbers for play. A dark night: fire illumination and flares. The defenders wear the M1952 flak vest; the Chinese attack with burp guns (submachine guns) and grenades.

Landing zone X-Ray, 14 November 1965

  • The armies: United States and North Vietnamese.
  • Fought for: the landing zone, attacked by the North Vietnamese.
  • The field: 160 by 130 hexes of 10 m, about 1,600 by 1,130 m, north at the top.
  • The weather: Fair, calm or light air.
  • Wounds: Vietnam 1965-70 - hospitalized wounded.
  • On the travel map: Ia Drang, 1965 (X-Ray and Albany), at Landing zone X-Ray.
  • The record: the fight lasted about 1346 exchanges (a minute each).

The campaign

By 1965 the Viet Cong held much of the South Vietnamese countryside, with North Vietnamese regulars of the People's Army of Vietnam (PAVN) behind them. General Westmoreland had won promises of about 300,000 American troops, and the build-up came that summer. Among the first to arrive was the 1st Cavalry Division (Airmobile), formed from the 11th Air Assault Division (Test) to try out war by helicopter. It set up its base at An Khe.

In the Central Highlands the PAVN's B3 Front, under Major General Chu Huy Mân, had the 32nd, 33rd and 66th Regiments. On 19 October 1965 the 33rd attacked the Special Forces camp at Plei Me while the 32nd lay in wait for the relief column. The camp held with air support. A South Vietnamese column was ambushed on the evening of 23 October, fought its way on, and reached the camp at dusk on the 25th. The North Vietnamese fell back west, towards the Chu Pong massif and Cambodia.

The 1st Cavalry Division went after them. On 13 November Colonel Thomas Brown of the 3rd Brigade ordered Lieutenant Colonel Harold Moore to make an air assault at the foot of the Chu Pong the next morning. Moore's 1st Battalion, 7th Cavalry should have had about 750 to 765 men; it had about 450. Sixteen Hueys would carry it in from Plei Me, about a company at a time, on a round trip that Galloway puts at 35 minutes. Waiting on the massif, though the Americans did not know it, were the 7th and 9th Battalions of the 66th Regiment.

The places

  • Landing zone X-Ray: a clearing about 100 m across that could take about eight helicopters at once.
  • The dry creek bed: beside the clearing, where A Company met the North Vietnamese coming down.
  • The termite hill: the bare termite mound on which Moore set his command post.
  • The knoll: a rise about 100 m beyond B Company's line, where its 2nd Platoon was cut off.
  • The Chu Pong massif: the high ground to the west, from which the North Vietnamese came down.
  • Landing zone Falcon: the guns that fired for X-Ray; Crandall's pilots shifted their supply runs there to shorten them.
  • Plei Me: the Special Forces camp besieged in October, and the pick-up point for the lift.
  • Landing zone Victor: where the 2nd Battalion, 5th Cavalry landed on the 15th before marching to X-Ray.
  • Landing zone Albany: about 4 km north-north-east, where the 2nd Battalion, 7th Cavalry was ambushed after leaving X-Ray.

The leaders

  • Harold G. Moore (United States, 1st Battalion, 7th Cavalry): refused to leave his battalion when ordered to Saigon to brief Westmoreland.
  • John Herren (United States, B Company): led the first company in.
  • Henry Herrick (United States, 2nd Platoon, B Company): followed North Vietnamese into the scrub, was cut off, and was killed.
  • Clyde E. "Ernie" Savage (United States, sergeant, 2nd Platoon): a squad leader who took command of the cut-off platoon.
  • Ramon "Tony" Nadal (United States, A Company): fought along the creek bed.
  • Robert Edwards (United States, C Company): held the south side; badly wounded on the 15th.
  • Bruce Crandall (United States, major, A Company, 229th Assault Helicopter Battalion): led the lift, call sign "Ancient Serpent 6".
  • Myron Diduryk (United States, B Company, 2nd Battalion, 7th Cavalry): flew in at dusk.
  • Chu Huy Mân (North Vietnamese, B3 Front): commanded the PAVN in the highlands.
  • Nguyễn Hữu An (North Vietnamese, B3 Front forward command post): commanded the front's forward post and wrote a memoir of the campaign (2005).

The battle

Times here are local, South Vietnam time (GMT+8); no source read says which clock the Americans used, but their accounts read as local time. Hanoi kept GMT+7. After about 30 minutes of artillery, rockets and air strikes, the first of B Company landed at 10:48 on 14 November. The second lift, the rest of B and a platoon of A, came at 11:20. At about noon a squad caught an unarmed North Vietnamese deserter, who said there were three battalions on the mountain. At about 12:15 the first shots hit B Company's patrols beyond the creek bed.

At about 13:00 Herrick's 2nd Platoon followed North Vietnamese into the scrub and was cut off about 100 m from the rest of the company. Herrick was killed after passing command to Sergeant Carl Palmer, who was killed in turn. Savage took over because he was beside the radio, and he brought artillery down round the platoon. C Company landed at 13:32 and took the south and south-west. A Company's platoons met North Vietnamese coming down the creek bed. At 14:30 the last of C Company and the lead of D Company landed under fire, as 175 to 200 North Vietnamese charged C Company; that attack was over by 15:00. The rest of the battalion was in by 15:20.

At 15:45 Moore sent A and B Companies to bring in their wounded and reach the cut-off platoon. They were stopped by a machine gun on a termite hill. Lieutenant Walter Marm knocked it out with a light anti-tank rocket, grenades and his rifle, and was wounded; he later received the Medal of Honor. The push got no further. B Company of the 2nd Battalion, 7th Cavalry, under Diduryk, began landing at about 17:00 and was in by 18:00. In the night the North Vietnamese probed the perimeter in squads, and attacked the cut-off platoon three times, before midnight, at 03:15 and at 04:30.

The wounded went out on the helicopters that brought the men in. The medical evacuation ships came in on the first afternoon and pulled out under fire with only two casualties. Freeman later said that their rules let them land only at a landing zone that had been quiet for five minutes. The lift Hueys carried the wounded out instead, Crandall and Freeman flying in ammunition and water and taking out about 70 wounded that day. Captain Tom Metsker was hit and killed while helping the wounded D Company commander, Captain Ray Lefebvre, onto a Huey.

At about 06:50 on the 15th some 200 North Vietnamese attacked C Company's side. Soon after 07:55, when the perimeter was marked with coloured smoke, an American F-100 dropped napalm close to the command post. Galloway saw two engineers badly burned, and helped carry Private First Class Jimmy Nakayama, burned by it, to the aid station; Nakayama died two days later. A Company of the 2nd Battalion, 7th Cavalry came in at 09:10, and the attacks died down at about 10:00. The 2nd Battalion, 5th Cavalry marched in from Victor at 12:05, and that afternoon the cut-off platoon was reached. Before dawn on the 16th Diduryk's company beat off four attacks. That morning Moore's battalion pulled out to Pleiku.

Where the accounts disagree

  • The losses at X-Ray. Wikipedia, after Carland, gives 79 Americans killed and 121 wounded, as does Galloway in Stars and Stripes (79 killed, more than 120 wounded). Wikipedia gives Galloway elsewhere as 80 killed and 124 wounded. Seabrooke gives 70 killed.
  • The North Vietnamese dead. Moore's count was 634 bodies, which he revised down from 834, with 1,215 more estimated killed by artillery and air; he later said his count was too high. The PAVN's Central Highlands Front report of 1966, as Wikipedia gives it, admits 559 killed and 669 wounded across five engagements of the campaign.
  • The whole campaign. Hanyok, for the National Security Agency, gives about 3,500 North Vietnamese and about 300 Americans killed. Galloway, on army.mil, gives 234 Americans killed and over 1,200 North Vietnamese for X-Ray and Albany together. The official PAVN history claims 1,700 Americans put out of action.
  • The cut-off platoon. Wikipedia gives 29 men, of whom 9 were killed and 13 wounded. Savage's citation says it held for 26 hours, which would put the relief at about 15:30 on the 15th, as Wikipedia does.
  • The enemy. The deserter spoke of three battalions on the massif; Freeman remembered three regiments. Seabrooke names the 32nd, 33rd and 66th Regiments; Wikipedia, after Carland, the 9th Battalion of the 66th close to the landing zone.
  • The wounded flown out. Crandall's Medal of Honor citation gives 22 flights but no count of wounded. Military Times and Seabrooke say about 70 or more than 70 for Crandall and Freeman together; HistoryLink says more than 75; Freeman's citation credits him with about 30.
  • When the shooting began. Wikipedia has the first shots at about 12:15; Seabrooke, after Freeman, has the shooting begin about 90 minutes after the landing.

Ancient Serpent 6

Major Bruce Crandall led the 16 Hueys that put Moore's battalion into X-Ray. When the landing zone came under fire, the medical evacuation helicopters would not go in, and Captain Tony Nadal radioed that he had 12 wounded and nobody to take them. Crandall took out his door gunner and weapons to save weight and went in unarmed. Captain Ed Freeman, his wingman, was the one volunteer to go with him. Crandall flew 22 flights that day, Freeman 14, bringing in ammunition and water and taking out the wounded. Freeman later reckoned his helicopter took more than 50 rounds, and that he flew for fourteen and a half hours. Both received the Distinguished Service Cross, later raised to the Medal of Honor: Freeman in 2001, Crandall in 2007.

How the field is drawn

Landing zone X-Ray on the afternoon of 14 November 1965, at 10 m a hex: 160 x 130 hexes, about 1600 m east to west and 1130 m north to south, north at the top: the clearing right of middle (the landing zone, H), the dry creek bed west of it, the lower slopes of the Chu Pong massif on the left, the knoll where B Company's 2nd Platoon was cut off up to the north-west. Light cover (scrub, key o): the tall elephant grass among the scrub trees (woods) round the clearing. The clearing, the creek bed, the knoll and the slopes are drawn by hand to the shape the accounts give, not traced from any map; the deployment is mid-afternoon of the 14th, as D Company was coming in, in our own words, with round numbers for play. Scrub trees, tall elephant grass and termite hills all round (woods, scrub, rough). D Company, and B Company of the 2nd Battalion at dusk, come in by air at the landing zone, 80 men an exchange, while the North Vietnamese are not on top of it; a hot landing zone costs men.

1 The fight at the creek bed About 13:35: B, A and C Companies are engaged and B Company's 2nd Platoon is cut off on the knoll.
56 D Company lands 14:30: the last of C Company and the lead of D Company land under fire.

Hill 875, Dak To, 19 November 1967

  • The armies: United States and ARVN and North Vietnamese.
  • Fought for: the crest of Hill 875, attacked by the United States and ARVN.
  • The field: 120 by 140 hexes of 10 m, about 1,200 by 1,210 m, north at the top.
  • The weather: Fair, calm or light air.
  • Wounds: Vietnam 1965-70 - hospitalized wounded.
  • On the travel map: Dak To, 1967 (the base to Hill 875), at Hill 875.
  • The record: the fight lasted about 5131 exchanges (a minute each).

The campaign

In the second half of 1967 the North Vietnamese fought a string of actions close to South Vietnam's borders: at Con Thien, Song Be, Loc Ninh, Dak To and later Khe Sanh. Wikipedia, after the American official histories, calls these the border battles, and says their aim was to draw American and South Vietnamese troops away from the cities before the Tet offensive. Round Dak To, in Kontum province, the 4th Infantry Division under Major General William Peers, the 173rd Airborne Brigade and South Vietnamese units had fought through the summer in Operation Greeley.

In October American intelligence saw North Vietnamese regiments moving north from Pleiku into Kontum, and gathered as the PAVN 1st Division. On 3 November a North Vietnamese sergeant, Vu Hong, gave himself up and described the plan. The 66th Regiment was to make the main attack south-west of Dak To, the 32nd to block to the south, the independent 24th to the north-east, and the 174th to be held in the north-west, with the 40th Artillery Regiment in support. A captured B3 Front document said the aim was to destroy a major American unit. American and South Vietnamese reinforcements came in under Operation MacArthur.

Through early November the Americans fought for one fortified hill after another: Hill 823, Hill 724, Hill 1338 and others. On 15 November mortars hit the ammunition and fuel dumps at the Dak To airstrip, and more than 1,100 tons of ammunition were destroyed. After that the North Vietnamese began to draw off to the south-west. The 174th Regiment, still fresh, moved west past Ben Het to cover the withdrawal of the 66th and 32nd. When a Mobile Strike Force company met strong resistance near Hill 875, Brigadier General Leo Schweiter of the 173rd ordered the 2nd Battalion, 503rd Infantry to take it.

The places

  • Dak To base and airstrip: the brigades' base; its ammunition dump blew up on 15 November.
  • Ben Het: the Special Forces camp near the border, with Fire Support Base 12 close by.
  • Fire Support Base 16: from which the 4th Battalion, 503rd Infantry was sent to relieve the 2nd.
  • Hill 823: where B Company, 4th Battalion, 503rd Infantry, about 120 men, was landed alone and held.
  • Hills 724 and 1338: two of the hills where the 4th Infantry Division fought earlier in November.
  • Hill 875: a jungle hill well west of Dak To, its crest ringed with bunkers and trenches, with tunnels by which the defenders later got away.
  • The north slope: the way the 2nd Battalion went up.
  • The new landing zone: a clearing for one helicopter, cut about two-thirds of the way up the hill on the 21st (Lewis).

The leaders

  • William R. Peers (United States, 4th Infantry Division): commanded the American forces round Dak To.
  • Leo H. Schweiter (United States, 173rd Airborne Brigade): ordered the attack on Hill 875.
  • James Steverson (United States, 2nd Battalion, 503rd Infantry): directed the battalion from a command helicopter.
  • Harold Kaufman (United States, captain, C Company): commanded the battalion's companies on the hill, and was killed by the bomb on the 19th.
  • Kiley (United States, captain, A Company): killed when his company was overrun from behind.
  • Charles J. Watters (United States, chaplain, 173rd Support Battalion): a Catholic priest, killed on the evening of the 19th.
  • Carlos Lozada (United States, private first class, A Company): held the rear with a machine gun until he was killed.
  • James Johnson (United States, 4th Battalion, 503rd Infantry): sent his battalion to the relief.
  • Ron Leonard (United States, captain, B Company, 4th Battalion): led the first of the relief onto the hill.
  • 174th Regiment (North Vietnamese, the defenders): no source read for this page names its commander. Wikipedia names Hoàng Minh Thảo as the North Vietnamese commander for the whole battle.

The battle

Times are local, South Vietnam time (GMT+8); Hanoi kept GMT+7. The 2nd Battalion spent the night of 18 November at the foot of the hill. On the morning of the 19th three companies, about 330 men by Wikipedia and about 290 by Scott, moved to their start line at 09:43. C and D Companies led up the north slope, with two platoons of A behind. At 10:30, within 300 m of the crest, machine guns, B-40 rockets and recoilless rifles opened on them from bunkers. D Company's point man was shot, and an aidman was killed. The attacks on the bunkers stalled, and Kaufman pulled the companies into a perimeter on the slope.

At about 14:30 (Scott says about 14:00) a North Vietnamese force waiting at the foot of the hill, by Wikipedia the 2nd Battalion of the 174th, struck A Company from the west along a trail. It overran A Company's command post; Kiley was among the dead. Lozada held the rear with his M60 and was killed; he received the Medal of Honor after his death. The battalion was now surrounded, with the enemy above and below. Six Hueys trying to bring in supplies that afternoon were shot down or badly damaged.

At 18:58, as Kaufman met his officers at dusk under a lone tree, an American aircraft dropped two bombs. One fell outside. The other burst in the trees over the command group, among the wounded and the medics gathered there. It killed 42 men and wounded 45. Kaufman was among the dead, and so was Watters, who had spent the afternoon going out under fire to bring in wounded. Lieutenants and sergeants took over what was left.

The wounded could not be got out. Scott says the medics ran out of dressings and used towels and T-shirts; one Huey hovered long enough to lift out five of the worst hurt, and another was driven off. On the 20th the 4th Battalion came up through sniper and mortar fire, and only reached the perimeter at nightfall. On the 21st a one-helicopter landing zone was cut on the slope, and the wounded began to go out, the 173rd lifting out its wounded from this fight for the first time; the helicopter pilot Lewis says Dustoff helicopters got in on the 22nd. The two battalions attacked on the afternoon of the 21st and reached the trenches but were called back at dark. On the 22nd the hilltop was bombed and shelled bare. At about 11:00 on 23 November they went up again and took the crest in about half an hour. The North Vietnamese had gone, leaving some bodies and weapons.

Where the accounts disagree

  • The bomb. Wikipedia, after Murphy, gives a Marine A-4 Skyhawk flown by Lieutenant Colonel Richard Taber, two 250 lb Snakeye bombs, at 18:58. Scott, after the after-action reports, says a propeller-driven aircraft and two 500 lb bombs. Lewis, a helicopter pilot at Dak To, says an F-4 and two 500-pounders. An anonymous 4th Battalion account says an Air Force fighter at about 20:00. The game keeps 18:58.
  • How many went up. Wikipedia gives 330 men in three companies; Scott about 290; Columbia magazine about 300.
  • Who held the hill. The 2nd Battalion went up expecting one company, says the Virtual Wall, and met two regiments. Columbia says a regiment of about 2,000. Wikipedia and Scott name the 174th Regiment.
  • The American losses. Wikipedia gives the 2nd Battalion 87 killed, 130 wounded and 3 missing, and the 4th 28 killed, 123 wounded and 4 missing. An unofficial count given by the Virtual Wall and the anonymous account has 158 killed, 33 missing and 411 wounded evacuated for the two battalions. The Virtual Wall lists 125 men who died in connection with the battle.
  • The North Vietnamese losses. Scott says about 22 bodies were found on the crest and the 174th lost more than half its strength. A Vietnamese account in Sài Gòn Giải Phóng (2021) says about 200 of the regiment died round Dak To and Tan Canh, and claims more than 4,000 Americans and South Vietnamese put out of action and 13 aircraft shot down. For the whole Dak To battle the US Army claimed 1,644 killed by body count; a PAVN report gives about 450 killed and 1,089 wounded.
  • The attack from behind. Wikipedia gives 14:30; Scott about 14:00.
  • The relief. Scott, in a hard-to-read scan, puts the first of the 4th Battalion on the hill at 17:30; the anonymous account gives about 16:00 for B Company and 20:00 to 20:30 for the others, on the 20th.
  • Who led. Scott faults both battalion commanders for directing the fight from helicopters rather than on the ground.

The chaplain

Charles Watters, a Catholic priest from New Jersey, was 40. He had made the only mass combat jump of the war with the 2nd Battalion, 503rd Infantry, in February 1967, and had stayed on in Vietnam beyond his year. On the morning of 19 November he said Mass for the battalion before it went up Hill 875. Through the afternoon, unarmed, he went out of the perimeter under fire to carry in wounded men and give the last rites to the dying; his citation says he went out three times. At dusk he was among the wounded in the middle of the perimeter, helping the medics, when the bomb burst overhead. He was killed. In 1969 his brothers received his Medal of Honor, the first given to an Army chaplain since the Civil War.

How the field is drawn

Hill 875 near Dak To on 19 November 1967, at 10 m a hex: 120 x 140 hexes, about 1200 m east to west and 1210 m north to south, north at the top: the crest below the middle, ringed with bunkers and trenches, the north slope above it shattered bamboo and fallen trees, jungle all round. The hill, the slopes, the bunkers and the trenches are drawn by hand to the shape the accounts give, not traced from any map; the deployment is the attack going up, in our own words, with round numbers for play. Fair and dry: the dry season had begun.

Hill 861A, Khe Sanh, 5 February 1968

  • The armies: United States and ARVN and North Vietnamese.
  • Fought for: the top of Hill 861A, attacked by the North Vietnamese.
  • The field: 140 by 120 hexes of 10 m, about 1,400 by 1,040 m, north at the top.
  • The weather: Fog, calm or light air, night.
  • Wounds: Vietnam 1965-70 - hospitalized wounded.
  • On the travel map: Khe Sanh, 1968 (the base and its hills), at Hill 861A.

The campaign

Khe Sanh combat base stood on a plateau in the far north-west of South Vietnam, near the border with Laos and below the Demilitarized Zone. Colonel David E. Lownds took over the 26th Marines there in August 1967. In early January 1968 American intelligence reported two, perhaps three, North Vietnamese divisions moving into the area: the 325C Division to the north and the 304th to the south. On 16 and 17 January Lieutenant Colonel Heath's 2nd Battalion, 26th Marines flew in and took post on Hill 558, north of the base.

The siege began on the night of 20/21 January. About 300 North Vietnamese attacked K Company, 3/26 Marines on Hill 861; they broke into the position and were driven out by 05:30, leaving 47 dead. At 05:30 on 21 January the shelling of the base began. One of the first rounds set off the main ammunition dump, which held more than 1,500 tons. Khe Sanh village was attacked the same day and given up. The Marines lost 14 killed and 43 wounded that day.

From then on the base and its hill outposts lived on what came by air: C-130s and C-123s onto the strip or by parachute, and helicopters out to the hills. On 22 January E Company, 2/26 moved from Hill 558 to a ridge north-east of Hill 861, which the Marines called 861 Alpha, to cover the battalion's flank. On the night of 30/31 January the Tet Offensive began across South Vietnam, but the expected main blow at Khe Sanh did not come.

The places

  • Khe Sanh combat base: the airstrip, bunkers and guns on the plateau, held by the 26th Marines, 1/9 Marines from 22 January and the 37th ARVN Ranger Battalion from 27 January.
  • Hill 861A: the knoll north-east of Hill 861 held by E Company, 2/26 from 22 January; it closed the gap in observation between Hill 861 and the battalion on Hill 558.
  • Hill 861: the outpost of K Company, 3/26, attacked on the first night of the siege.
  • Hill 558: north of the base, covering a valley along the Rao Quan river; 2/26's main position.
  • Hill 881 South: a Marine outpost held by I Company, 3/26, with three 105 mm howitzers.
  • Hill 881 North: the North Vietnamese-held twin of 881 South, retaken on 14 April.
  • Hill 950: a Marine outpost from 1966 to 1969; men of 1/26 held it through the siege.
  • Khe Sanh village: the village by the base, attacked and given up on 21 January.
  • Lang Vei: the Special Forces camp, held by Americans and Bru irregulars, overrun by tanks on 7 February.

The leaders

  • David E. Lownds (US, 26th Marines): colonel commanding the base. He ordered a red alert when 861A was attacked.
  • Heath (US, 2/26 Marines): lieutenant colonel; his battalion held Hill 558 and lent E Company to 861A. The sources read give no first name.
  • Earle G. Breeding (US, E Company, 2/26): captain. He shifted his men to stiffen the broken line and called artillery and mortar fire close round the hill; he received the Silver Star.
  • Donald E. R. Shanley (US, 1st Platoon, E Company): first lieutenant. He pulled his platoon back to its alternate positions and led the counter-attack at 05:00.
  • John A. Hennelly (US, 1st Battalion, 13th Marines): lieutenant colonel commanding the base's artillery battalion.
  • Mirza "Harry" Baig (US, 26th Marines): captain. He later judged that the artillery had kept the attackers' reserves away from the hill.
  • Tom Eichler (US, corporal, E Company): Fixler says he killed three men hand to hand and destroyed a machine gun inside the wire; he received the Silver Star.
  • Trần Quý Hai (North Vietnamese, local commander): major general commanding the forces round Khe Sanh, with Lê Quang Đạo as political commissar.
  • Võ Nguyên Giáp (North Vietnamese): Wikipedia names him the theatre commander.

The battle

Times are local, as the American accounts give them. Shortly after 03:00 on 5 February the North Vietnamese opened on the combat base with rockets, guns and mortars. Soon after, Captain Breeding reported about 200 North Vietnamese coming through the wire on top of Hill 861A. Sappers had cut lanes, and the infantry came up behind them under mortar and small arms fire. There were no sensors near the hill to give warning. Lownds put the whole regiment on red alert, and the 1st Battalion, 13th Marines answered with a heavy barrage round the hill.

The attackers broke into the 1st Platoon's sector on the north of the perimeter. Lieutenant Shanley drew his platoon back to its alternate positions, and the North Vietnamese held part of the trench line. The Marines threw CS gas grenades; Fixler, a lance corporal in the company, remembers the gas blowing back over them, so that men fought in masks and could hardly see. At about 05:00 Shanley led the platoon out of its holes in a counter-attack. The fighting was hand to hand, with knives, bayonets, rifle butts and fists. The North Vietnamese fell back, gathered again, and made a second, half-hearted attack, which was beaten off before dawn.

Through the night the base's guns fired round the hill. Baig later counted almost 2,000 rounds from the 1st Battalion, 13th Marines alone, and thought this fire had stopped the North Vietnamese reserves from joining the attack. Fixler says the Marines were also hit by their own shells more than once.

At first light a sweep of the slope and the perimeter found more than 100 North Vietnamese dead. E Company lost 7 killed and 24 wounded (Shulimson). Fixler describes the wounded patched up by the corpsmen, wrapped in ponchos and carried to a staging area by the landing zone, to be flown out by helicopter to a field hospital.

Two days later, on the night of 6/7 February, Lang Vei was overrun by PT-76 tanks and infantry. On 8 February a North Vietnamese battalion partly overran A Company, 1/9 Marines' outpost west of the base. The siege went on until Operation Pegasus reached the base on 8 April.

Where the accounts disagree

  • The date. Shulimson, the Khe Sanh Veterans' chronology and Fixler put the attack on 5 February. Wikipedia's article on the 325th Division gives 3 February.
  • The clock. South Vietnam kept GMT+8 from 1960 to 1975; North Vietnam kept GMT+7 from 1 January 1968 (Wikipedia, "Time in Vietnam"). The American times here are taken to be South Vietnamese local time, though no account says so.
  • The hour. The game opens at 03:05. Shulimson, as read for this page, says only that the shelling began around 03:00 and that Breeding's report came shortly after.
  • The attackers. Breeding reported about 200 men. The Khe Sanh Veterans' chronology calls it a North Vietnamese battalion, and Wikipedia a battalion of the 325C Division. No account read for this page names the battalion or its regiment, and no North Vietnamese account of the fight was found in English.
  • The losses. Shulimson gives E Company 7 dead and 24 wounded. Fixler gives 7 dead and at least 30 seriously wounded. Shulimson has more than 100 North Vietnamese dead counted; Fixler and the Khe Sanh Veterans' chronology give 109. Breeding's citation speaks of more than 100 killed or captured.
  • When E Company took the hill. The Khe Sanh Veterans' chronology and Shore put the move to 861A on 22 January, about a week after 2/26 reached Hill 558. Wikipedia's article on the battle has E Company on 861A after 2/26 arrived. One sentence in Shulimson, as read for this page, seemed to say the company had occupied the hill that same morning; we could not check it against the printed page.
  • Where. Breeding's citation places the action at "Hill 861"; the other accounts use 861A.

Find my hand

Lance Corporal Barry Fixler of E Company was in the trenches on Hill 861A when the North Vietnamese came through the wire before dawn on 5 February. He later wrote that artillery, rockets, mortars, small arms, bayonets and tear gas all came at once, and that the gas blew back into the Marines' own faces. It took all night to clear the hill. The wounded were wrapped in ponchos and carried down to the landing zone for the helicopters. One of them asked Fixler to find his hand. Fixler counted 109 North Vietnamese dead on the slopes, spread over perhaps two acres. Seven Marines of the company had been killed.

Hue: the new city, 4-6 February 1968

  • The armies: United States and ARVN and North Vietnamese.
  • Fought for: the provincial headquarters, attacked by the United States and ARVN.
  • The field: 150 by 110 hexes of 10 m, about 1,500 by 950 m, north at the top.
  • The weather: Rain, breeze from the north-east.
  • Wounds: Vietnam 1965-70 - hospitalized wounded.
  • On the travel map: Hue, 1968 (the city and Phu Bai), at Hue, the new city (south bank).
  • The record: the fight lasted about 3301 exchanges (a minute each).

The campaign

Many ARVN soldiers were on leave for the Tet truce of 1968. Shortly after midnight on 30 January attacks went in early in parts of I and II Corps, and the truce was cancelled. At about 03:00 on 31 January the main offensive struck: by one count about 77,000 North Vietnamese and NLF (Viet Cong) troops, against more than 100 towns and cities, among them 36 of the 44 provincial capitals. Hanoi hoped for a general uprising. It did not come.

In October 1967 Major General Trần Văn Quang, commanding the Tri-Thien-Hue region, was ordered to take Hue at Tet; Camp says he asked for more time and was refused. A Hue City Front was formed with two wings. The 6th Regiment took the Citadel, north of the Perfume River. The 4th Regiment took the new city to the south, with the provincial headquarters, the prison and the MACV compound as its objectives. Sappers came in on 28-30 January dressed as peasants. The occupiers carried lists of officials, officers and others to be rounded up. When no uprising came, Bowden writes, the aim became to stay close to the Americans, so that they could not use their firepower freely.

Early on 31 January they took most of the city. The ARVN 1st Division held its headquarters at Mang Ca, in the Citadel, and about 100 American advisers held the MACV compound south of the river. That morning A Company, 1st Battalion, 1st Marines was sent up Highway 1 from Phu Bai. It was ambushed at the edge of the city and its captain, Gordon Batcheller, was badly wounded; Gunnery Sergeant John Canley took over. Lieutenant Colonel Marcus Gravel came up with a relief force and reached the compound at about 15:15. An attempt that afternoon to cross the bridge into the Citadel was driven back. The two Marine companies lost 10 killed and 56 wounded that day.

Over the next three days 2/5 Marines came in: F Company by helicopter on 1 February, H Company by convoy on the 2nd, and the battalion commander, Lieutenant Colonel Ernest Cheatham, with Colonel Stanley Hughes of the 1st Marines on the 3rd. The university was taken on 2 February. Hughes gave 1/1 the task of keeping Highway 1 open and 2/5 the task of clearing the blocks along the river bank. Cheatham was sent bazookas, 106 mm recoilless rifles on Mule carriers, flamethrowers and tear gas. On the evening of 3 February the limits on supporting fire south of the river were lifted.

The places

  • The Truong Tien bridge (Camp: the Nguyen Hoang bridge): the road bridge into the Citadel, which Gravel's men tried to cross on 31 January; blown on 7 February.
  • The MACV compound: the advisers' walled compound, about 300 by 200 yards, a block and a half south of the river by Highway 1.
  • Hue University: across from the compound, by the bridge; 2/5's command post and starting line.
  • The Treasury, the post office and the Public Health building: the first strong points in 2/5's way, taken on 4 February.
  • The Jeanne d'Arc school: the Catholic school and chapel cleared by A Company, 1/1 on 4 February.
  • The hospital: a complex of buildings, taken on 5 and 6 February.
  • The provincial headquarters: a two-storey building inside walls, the 4th Regiment's command post, taken on 6 February.
  • The An Cuu bridge and Phu Bai: the bridge on Highway 1 over the Phu Cam canal, blown on the night of 4 February, and the Marine base to the south from which the reinforcements came and the wounded went back.

The leaders

  • Foster C. LaHue (US, Task Force X-Ray): brigadier general; he wrote that the first moves were made "with limited information".
  • Stanley S. Hughes (US, 1st Marines): colonel in charge of the fighting south of the river from 3 February.
  • Ernest C. Cheatham (US, 2/5 Marines): lieutenant colonel; he marked targets for the 106 mm guns with tracer himself.
  • Marcus Gravel (US, 1/1 Marines): lieutenant colonel; reached the MACV compound on 31 January.
  • Ronald Christmas (US, H Company, 2/5): captain; he received the Navy Cross for 5 February at the hospital, where he directed a tank's fire from on top of it.
  • John L. Canley and Alfredo Gonzalez (US, A Company, 1/1): gunnery sergeant and sergeant; Gonzalez was killed at the Jeanne d'Arc school on 4 February.
  • Frank A. Thomas Jr. (US, gunnery sergeant, H Company): Nolan has him raise the flag over the provincial headquarters.
  • Trần Văn Quang (North Vietnamese, Tri-Thien-Hue region): major general who planned the attack on Hue.
  • Nguyen Trong Dan (North Vietnamese, 6th Regiment): lieutenant colonel commanding in the Citadel. Camp names the 4th Regiment's commander, in the new city, only as "Lieutenant Colonel Nguyen Van".

The battle

Times are local, as the American accounts give them. At about 07:00 on 4 February 2/5 went for the Treasury. A 106 mm gun on a Mule knocked out a heavy machine gun while Cheatham marked the target with tracer. H Company took the Public Health building and fired from it, with a 106 mm in a second-floor room. Captain Michael Downs's F Company attacked from a Catholic school across the street, and Lance Corporal Richard Carter fired more than 100 rockets from a 3.5-inch launcher into gates and walls. Gas from E-8 launchers, rigged by the battalion's executive officer, helped clear the Treasury, and a tank came up in support. By about 17:00 the Treasury, the post office and the Public Health building were held. Gas thrown down a bunker by the post office that evening left 24 North Vietnamese dead inside.

Next door A Company, 1/1 cleared the Jeanne d'Arc school and its chapel. Some of the Treasury gas drifted over them; they had no masks. Gonzalez was killed by a rocket. More than half of the company's 147 men were killed or wounded that day. That night sappers blew the An Cuu bridge, cutting the road to Phu Bai.

On 5 February 2/5 pushed on to the hospital. By the afternoon the Marines were inside the complex, fighting room by room with an Ontos in support, and the first building was cleared at about 16:30. Christmas crossed open ground to a tank hit by two rockets and directed its fire standing on it. The province chief, Lieutenant Colonel Phạm Văn Khoa, was found in the hospital.

On 6 February the hospital was cleared and H Company went for the provincial headquarters. Gas blew away on the river breeze; a tank was hit by two rockets and kept going. An Ontos moving up to blast the wall was knocked out by a B-40. A 106 mm on a Mule breached the building, and the Marines cleared it room by room, then the spider holes round it. Nolan says that a little after 14:00 Gunnery Sergeant Thomas and two others pulled down the North Vietnamese flag and raised an American one. South Vietnamese law did not allow it to fly alone, and it came down the next morning. The prison nearby was found empty. Hanger says resistance in the southern city largely collapsed once the headquarters fell.

The wounded were dragged back across the streets by those less badly hurt, or brought in by tanks. On 31 January the advisers' dispensary took the first casualties, abandoned civilian vehicles served as ambulances, and the worst wounded went out by truck or, at night, by a Marine CH-46 that landed in the fog. Later, wounded men such as Carter were flown to Phu Bai by helicopter, though the low cloud often kept aircraft away. Hanger counts 38 Marines killed and 320 wounded in clearing the new city. During the occupation the PAVN and NLF rounded up and killed civilians and prisoners, many of them named on their lists; almost 2,800 bodies were recovered from mass graves in 1968 and 1969, and estimates of the dead run from several hundred (Porter) to about 6,000 (Wikipedia, after Pike, Vennema and others).

Where the accounts disagree

  • The clock. South Vietnam kept GMT+8 from 1960 to 1975 and North Vietnam GMT+7 from 1 January 1968 (Wikipedia, "Time in Vietnam"). The American times are taken here as South Vietnamese local time; no account says so.
  • The signal. Wikipedia, after Pike, has a flare start the attack at 02:33 on 31 January; Camp has the flare and the rockets at about 03:40, which Wikipedia, after Villard, gives as the time the rockets hit the new city.
  • The flag. Nolan has Thomas and two other Marines raise it a little after 14:00, on Christmas's order. Gurske, writing a day-by-day account online, has Privates First Class Walter Kaczmarek and Alan McDonald pull down the Viet Cong flag at 16:03, another Marine raising the American one. Wikipedia, after Shulimson, says it was ordered down for want of a South Vietnamese flag beside it.
  • Who took the Treasury. Nolan has F Company assault the Treasury with H Company firing from the Public Health building. Gurske has H Company open the attack on the Treasury at 07:00 and F Company clear it. Hanger has the Treasury and post office taken on 3 February and given up for want of men, before the attack of the 4th.
  • The province chief. Wikipedia, after Bowden, says the Marines rescued Phạm Văn Khoa at the hospital. Gurske says they doubted his story at first and held him.
  • The losses on 6 February. Nolan has two Marines killed at the provincial headquarters; Gurske, one killed in the whole southern sector that day.
  • The whole battle. Bowden, as reviewed in Studies in Intelligence, gives 250 Americans killed and 1,554 wounded, 458 ARVN killed and about 2,700 wounded, 2,400 to 5,000 North Vietnamese and NLF dead, and about 8,000 civilian dead. Wikipedia gives the North Vietnamese and NLF dead as 1,042 to 5,133.
  • Canley's award. Camp gives Canley the Navy Cross; Wikipedia says he and Gonzalez both received the Medal of Honor.
  • The enemy units. Camp gives the 4th Regiment the 804th and K4B Battalions; Wikipedia, after Villard, names the 804th and 810th, and after Bowden the 815th, which stopped the Marines on 2 February.

Somehow or other

On the afternoon of 6 February H Company, 2/5 Marines took the provincial headquarters, which the 4th Regiment had used as its command post. A flag of the other side flew over it. Marines pulled it down, and one of them had brought an American flag. It went up while photographers and a television crew filmed. Raising it was against the rules: South Vietnamese law said an American flag must fly beside a South Vietnamese one. Cheatham let it stand for the day. Hammel, quoted by Gurske, gives his report to Phu Bai: the headquarters was taken and "somehow or other, an American flag is flying over there". It came down the next morning.

How the field is drawn

The new city of Hue, south of the Perfume River, on 4-6 February 1968, at 10 m a hex: 150 x 110 hexes, about 1500 m east to west and 950 m north to south, north at the top: the river along the top with its bridge into the Citadel, Le Loi street and the park along the bank, Highway 1 coming up from the An Cuu bridge on the Phu Cam canal along the bottom, and between them blocks of houses and the stone public buildings: the MACV compound, the university, the provincial headquarters, the Treasury, the hospital and the prison. The streets, blocks and buildings are drawn by hand to that pattern, not traced from any map or photograph; the deployment is the Marines attacking east, in our own words, with round numbers for play. The public buildings are tall buildings (tall buildings) and the houses buildings, with rubble where the shells fell; tanks keep to the streets. Cold drizzle and low cloud.

Hamburger Hill (Dong Ap Bia), 20 May 1969

  • The armies: United States and ARVN and North Vietnamese.
  • Fought for: the summit of Hill 937 (Hamburger Hill), attacked by the United States and ARVN.
  • The field: 140 by 140 hexes of 10 m, about 1,400 by 1,210 m, north at the top.
  • The weather: Overcast, calm or light air.
  • Wounds: Vietnam 1965-70 - hospitalized wounded.
  • On the travel map: Hamburger Hill, 1969 (the A Shau valley), at Dong Ap Bia (Hill 937).

The campaign

The A Shau valley runs about 45 km along the Laotian border in south-western Thua Thien province. The North Vietnamese had held it since they overran the Special Forces camp there in 1966. It held their Base Area 611 and carried a road from the Ho Chi Minh Trail towards Hue and the coast. In early 1969 the 9th Marines' Operation Dewey Canyon found North Vietnamese roads and supply dumps. By March American intelligence saw the North Vietnamese rebuilding.

Lieutenant General Richard G. Stilwell of XXIV Corps ordered a raid into the valley, not an attempt to hold it. This was Operation Apache Snow. Major General Melvin Zais's 101st Airborne Division (Airmobile) was to destroy the North Vietnamese 29th Regiment. Colonel Joseph B. Conmy Jr.'s 3rd Brigade had three battalions: the 2nd Battalion, 501st Infantry, the 1st Battalion, 506th Infantry and the 3rd Battalion, 187th Infantry. Two battalions of the ARVN 1st Division were under its command. The plan was a reconnaissance in force, and intelligence was poor: the North Vietnamese moved by night and kept off the radio.

On 10 May, after a 74-minute bombardment of about 30 possible landing zones, the first Hueys landed at 07:10 (Willbanks). Lieutenant Colonel Weldon F. Honeycutt's 3rd Battalion, 187th Infantry landed about 2,000 m north-west of Dong Ap Bia, Hill 937, and set off through the jungle to clear it. The hill was held by the 29th Regiment, which the North Vietnamese called the 3rd Regiment of the 324th Division. Its 7th and 8th Battalions were dug in on the mountain in bunkers, trenches and tunnels.

The places

  • The A Shau valley: a floor of elephant grass between mountains under double and triple canopy jungle, a mile or two from Laos.
  • Dong Ap Bia (Hill 937): a solitary massif about 1.9 km from the border, 937 m high. The Montagnards called it "the mountain of the crouching beast".
  • The landing zone: about 2,000 m north-west of the summit, where the 3rd Battalion, 187th Infantry came in.
  • Hill 916: a peak on a ridge running south from the summit. Traas puts it about 1,000 m south-west; bunkers there stopped the 1st Battalion, 506th Infantry on 16 May.
  • Hill 900: the end of the spur running south-east, where the 1st Battalion, 506th Infantry was pinned on 18 May.
  • Firebase Airborne: the guns on a ridge about 7 km north-east. Two North Vietnamese battalions attacked it before dawn on 13 May.
  • Laos: across the border to the west, where the 29th Regiment's reinforcements came from and its survivors went.
  • The game's field: the summit and its upper slopes, with the north-west spur, the south spur and the eastern slope; the landing zones and Hills 900 and 916 lie off the board.

The leaders

  • Melvin Zais (United States, 101st Airborne Division): thought of stopping the attack on 18 May, then reinforced it.
  • Richard G. Stilwell (United States, XXIV Corps) and Creighton W. Abrams (United States, MACV): backed Zais in going on. Afterwards Abrams had to take more care of American lives.
  • Joseph B. Conmy Jr. (United States, 3rd Brigade): sent the 1st Battalion, 506th Infantry north on 13 May and ordered the two-battalion attack of 18 May.
  • Weldon F. Honeycutt (United States, 3rd Battalion, 187th Infantry): wounded on 15 May (Traas), he would not be evacuated. On 19 May he asked to keep his battalion in the fight, and Zais let him.
  • Robert J. Bower (United States, 1st Battalion, 506th Infantry): fought up from the south-west for four days. Wikipedia calls him John Bowers.
  • Robert L. German (United States, 2nd Battalion, 501st Infantry): landed north-east of the hill on 19 May.
  • Ngô Quang Trưởng (South Vietnamese, 1st Division): offered his 2nd Battalion, 3rd Regiment for the last attack.
  • Ma Vĩnh Lan (North Vietnamese, 29th Regiment): its commander by Wikipedia, with Kiều Tam Nguyên as political commissar. No other source read for this page names them.
  • Hồ Thị Đơm (North Vietnamese, local forces): a Pa Cô woman who, the Vietnamese press says, commanded a local company on Đồi A Bia. It gives no date.

The battle

On 11 May B Company met camouflaged bunkers; Traas gives 3 killed and 19 wounded. A second assault cleared the slope by 16:45, and helicopters took out the wounded that evening. Then a gunship fired on the battalion command post. It was the first of five times American aircraft hit the battalion. On 14 May three companies attacked. Willbanks counts a dozen killed and more than 80 wounded. On 15 May A and B Companies got within about 150 m of the summit, and a Cobra put rockets into B Company's command group. On 15 or 16 May the Associated Press reporter Jay Sharbutt reached the battalion. His stories gave the mountain its name in print.

On 18 May fighter-bombers struck from 08:00, then the artillery fired for an hour. The 3rd Battalion, 187th Infantry attacked from the north and the 1st Battalion, 506th Infantry from the south. D Company came within about 75 m of the top, fighting at a few metres, and lost all its officers. Then a rainstorm turned the bare slope to mud and the attack came back down. By the next day A and B Companies were at half strength, and C and D had lost 80%. Zais thought of calling off the attack. Instead, backed by Stilwell and Abrams, he brought in the 2nd Battalion, 501st Infantry and the ARVN 2nd Battalion, 3rd Regiment. He meant to relieve Honeycutt's battalion, but Honeycutt asked for one more company and got A Company of the 2nd Battalion, 506th Infantry. On 19 May helicopters put the new battalions down about 1,200 m north-east and south-east of the hill. By dark the 1st Battalion, 506th Infantry was within 200 m of the summit.

No account read says which clock the times on 20 May keep; South Vietnam kept UTC+8 and the North UTC+7. Air strikes and artillery pounded the summit for about two hours. Traas has the 3rd Battalion, 187th Infantry move off at 11:00. Mira says it met no fire until the second line of bunkers, about 75 m from the top, where rifles and rocket-propelled grenades opened on it. Specialist 4 Johnny Jackson went forward alone with his M60, and A Company followed him over the last 20 m. Traas says A Company was on the summit about 55 minutes after the start. Most of the North Vietnamese had gone. Willbanks says about two platoons, apparently ordered to stay, fought to the end. The others went down the western slopes towards Laos. The hill was secure by 17:00.

The wounded went out by helicopter. Where no helicopter could land, the 326th Medical Battalion's Eagle Dustoff crews lowered litters on hoists through the trees. Galloway puts about half the American losses down to fragments and 30% to bullets. Friendly fire killed 5 and wounded 53. On 21 May the 3rd Battalion, 187th Infantry flew out to rest at Eagle Beach, on the coast. Traas gives the cost as 70 Americans killed and 372 wounded, against 633 North Vietnamese dead counted.

The fight was news before it ended. On 20 May Senator Edward Kennedy called the attack "senseless and irresponsible" on the floor of the Senate; Senators George McGovern and Stephen Young joined him. Zais answered that the hill mattered only because the enemy was on it. On 5 June the order came to leave Dong Ap Bia, and about two weeks later North Vietnamese troops were reported back on it. Nixon told Abrams to fight with fewer American losses. On 8 June, at Midway, he announced the first withdrawal of 25,000 men.

Where the accounts disagree

  • The clock. No account read for this page says which clock its times keep. South Vietnam kept UTC+8 in 1969, North Vietnam UTC+7 (Wikipedia). The game uses the times as given.
  • When the last attack went in. Traas has the 3rd Battalion, 187th Infantry move off at 11:00 and reach the top 55 minutes later. Wikipedia, after the 101st's report, also starts it at 11:00, with the crest reached by noon. Willbanks starts it at 10:00 and has the summit at 11:45. All agree it was secure by 17:00.
  • Who was first on top. Traas, Willbanks and Mira put A Company of the 3rd Battalion, 187th Infantry first. Wiest, as Wikipedia gives him, says the ARVN 2nd Battalion, 3rd Regiment found a lightly held slope and reached the crest about 10:00, but was ordered off because the American artillery was about to fire on the summit.
  • The American losses. Traas and Willbanks give 70 killed and 372 wounded. Wikipedia, after the 101st's report, gives 56 killed, 367 wounded and 7 missing; History.com 72 killed; Galloway about 66 killed. The 3rd Battalion, 187th Infantry lost 39 killed and 290 wounded (Willbanks); Mira gives it 329 killed and wounded together.
  • The North Vietnamese losses. The American count was 633 bodies (Traas, Mira) or 630 (Wikipedia). Willbanks says a Special Forces patrol in Laos reported about 1,100 dead and wounded carried out; Galloway says trail-watchers counted over 1,200. The Vietnamese newspaper Sài Gòn Giải Phóng claims about 1,500 Americans killed; Wikipedia gives the PAVN claim as 1,500 killed and wounded.
  • The defenders. Wikipedia gives about 800 men in two battalions. Mira estimates the 29th Regiment at 1,200 to 1,800. Sài Gòn Giải Phóng names the defenders as the 3rd Regiment of the 324th Division, with local forces and militia, and says the Americans and South Vietnamese brought 13 battalions.
  • The fire on the command post. Traas says the gunship killed 1 and wounded 35 on 11 May; Willbanks 2 killed and 35 wounded; the HistoryNet timeline 2 killed and 25 wounded. In all, Wikipedia says, friendly fire killed 7 and wounded 53; Galloway says 5 and 53.
  • The bombardment. Willbanks and the HistoryNet timeline put over 20,000 shells, 272 air strikes, over 1 million pounds of bombs and 152,000 pounds of napalm before the attack of 20 May. Wikipedia gives the 20,000 rounds and 272 missions for the whole battle.
  • Hill 916. Wikipedia has the 1st Battalion, 506th Infantry take it on 15 May, Willbanks on the 16th; Traas has the battalion fired on from it on the 16th.
  • Was it worth it? Zais said the hill had no military value in itself; the enemy was there. Honeycutt argued that it overlooked a main North Vietnamese supply and staging area.

Dustoff 927

On 13 May wounded men of D Company, 3rd Battalion, 187th Infantry were pinned near a river at the foot of Hill 937. Dustoff 927, a Huey of the 326th Medical Battalion, came in over the trees and let down its hoist. First Lieutenant Gerald Torba was flying. The worst hurt, Private First Class George Pickel, was halfway up in a litter basket when a rocket-propelled grenade hit the rotor. The helicopter fell onto the men below and caught fire. The co-pilot, First Lieutenant Jerry Lee, the crew chief, Specialist 4 James Walters, and the medic, Specialist 4 James Margro, were killed, and so was Pickel. Torba was left on the hill and found about 17 hours later. He lost his left leg below the knee, stayed in the Army, and retired a lieutenant colonel in 1992.

How the field is drawn

The summit of Dong Ap Bia (Hill 937) on 20 May 1969, at 10 m a hex: 140 x 140 hexes, about 1400 m east to west and 1210 m north to south, north at the top: the summit in the middle, stripped to stumps and craters, with tiers of bunkers down its slopes, the spurs running down to the north-west and the south, blasted jungle and bamboo below. The hill, its spurs and the bunkers are drawn by hand to the shape the accounts give, not traced from any map; the deployment is the last assault, in our own words, with round numbers for play. Overcast, the slopes mud after days of rain.

A worked example: the squad

The Rules follow one medieval retinue. This chapter follows a US Army rifle squad in Vietnam through one night, with the same rules and the modules this book switches on and, where dice are rolled, the dice given. The team builder made the squad.

The squad

The team builder rolls a rifle squad. Ricky Garcia leads it: 3 terms, each a year of the war, so he is 21, with Command 90. Its machine gunner is Dennis Garcia, 2 terms, who fires the gun at 40% but defends at only 15%. Its grenadier is Daniel Miller, and its medic is John Washington, Leechcraft 41. 5 riflemen follow them. Their kit: M1 helmet, nylon flak vest (US Army M1952/M69, 1952-75).

On the field map

The squad: an ambush in the dark

The squad lies in extended order beside a trail on a dark night, gone to ground. No one can see to aim past 55 yards (50 m). Shots at the squad lose 15% for going to ground, and only 10% of the aimed ones find a man to aim at.

An enemy column comes down the trail. When the squad's gun opens fire, its muzzle flashes give it away: the enemy can now aim at its hex from up to 328 yards (300 m). The sergeant calls the company's mortars for illumination. It lands this exchange and lights the trail as by day for 2 exchanges, so his riflemen can aim.

In the roller

The heroes' wounds are rolled in full, as in the fight.

The squad: the gun

An enemy rifleman, a regular, fires his AK at Dennis at 50% and rolls 15: a margin of 35. Against a bullet, an arm takes a margin of 30 or more to be serious, so this one is serious. Dennis dodges at 15% and rolls 40: no.

The round strikes his upper arm (right), where his vest does not reach. It bleeds 2, pain 2, and the arm is hurt. The wound carries shock, so he makes a stop check: Nerve 60, less 2 steps of pain, gives 40. He rolls 22 and passes: he fights on.

But the machine gun takes both hands. With an arm hurt he cannot fire it, as in Wounds, so he can only defend. At 1 Blood a round, his 18 Blood lasts 18 rounds.

The squad: the grenade

A grenade bursts beside Daniel. The thrower's margin is 25 (he rolled 25). A fragment in the body is serious from a margin of 10, so this is serious, in his chest (left). But his vest, a nylon flak vest (M1952, M69), takes 2 steps off a fragment: it is stopped. Against a rifle round the same vest takes nothing.

The squad: the medic

In a quiet moment John crawls to the gun. He binds Dennis's arm at his Leechcraft 41 and rolls 12: he binds it, taking the bleeding down 2 steps to 0. The arm is still hurt (−20% to his attack with it), so another man takes the gun.

At dawn the squad carries him back. His wound goes onto the track as in Recovery.

For the GM

In a later war the heroes are the few men whose names the players know in a fight of hundreds. Keep the field map for the shape of the night and the roller for the moments that matter: a gunner hit, a medic crawling out, a vest that held.
